detail.abstract: When it comes to the various marketing activities that firms undertake to create and sustain value, just how broadly should they engage across the domain of marketing? Conceptualizing marketing breadth as the scope of a firm’s marketing activities, the current study proposes an empirical measure of this construct and examines its implications for firm value with a contingency framework. Greater breadth can provide a broader repertoire of marketing resources and capabilities and more flexibility to pursue market opportunities; it also can spread limited managerial attention thin and increase coordination demands. The authors create a text-based measure of the number of unique marketing concepts identified in a firm’s annual report and validate it using marketing, product market, and capital market outcomes. The results of the contingency model reveal that, on average, greater marketing breadth is associated with higher firm value, but this association also varies with lifecycle stage and market dynamics. In establishing marketing breadth as a distinct dimension of marketing strategy, this study highlights the importance of considering not only firms’ investments in specific marketing activities but also the breadth of activities they pursue.

detail.abstract: This article presents an expanded English research-paper version of an undergraduate thesis on the determinants of purchase decisions for Erigo, an Indonesian fashion brand. The manuscript relies only on the empirical information reported in the thesis and does not introduce unverified respondent data or reestimated statistics. The study investigates whether perceptions of a brand ambassador and brand trust are associated with purchase decisions among Generation Z respondents in Tonjong Village, Tajurhalang District, Bogor Regency, Indonesia. The source study employed a quantitative design, a five-point Likert questionnaire, and regression-based analysis on 100 respondents. The reported findings show that brand ambassador perceptions are positively associated with purchase decisions (R = 0.649; R² = 0.421; B = 0.856; t = 8.448; p < 0.001), and that brand trust is also positively associated with purchase decisions (R = 0.659; R² = 0.434; B = 0.732; t = 8.674; p < 0.001). In the multiple regression model, both predictors remain statistically significant, with brand ambassador (B = 0.430; β = 0.326; p = 0.018) and brand trust (B = 0.429; β = 0.386; p = 0.005), while the overall model explains 46.6% of the variance in the purchase-decision score (R = 0.683; R² = 0.466; adjusted R² = 0.455; F(2,97) = 42.382; p < 0.001). These findings are interpreted as correlational rather than causal. The manuscript also discusses the implications of the reported evidence, methodological limitations of the thesis, and directions for future research. The literature review is grounded in articles published in Scopus-indexed journals.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a network-based theory of personalized pricing in which consumers assess price fairness through comparisons with socially connected groups. A monopolist serves n observable consumer groups and chooses a vector of group-specific prices. Relative to a uniform-price benchmark, the price vector is represented by a personalization vector y ∈ R n. We model perceived unfairness as a quadratic network energy, U (y) = 1 2 y ⊤ Ly, where L is the weighted graph Laplacian of a consumer comparison network. Under linear group-level demand, the incremental operating profit has the exact quadratic form 2d ⊤ W y-y ⊤ W y, where W contains group demand slopes and d is the vector of deviations of group-specific monopoly prices from the uniform benchmark. With a convex quadratic implementation cost, the firm's problem is a strictly concave quadratic program subject to a convex network-trust constraint. We establish existence and uniqueness of the optimal personalized price vector, derive its Karush-Kuhn-Tucker characterization, and identify the multiplier on the trust constraint as the marginal value of relaxing the trust budget. When implementation costs are proportional to demand slopes, the solution admits an explicit spectral representation in the eigenbasis of the demand-normalized graph Laplacian. This representation shows that personalization is attenuated mode by mode according to the corresponding network eigenvalue. We also prove that adding a comparison link weakly reduces the firm's maximal attainable profit under a fixed trust budget, and we characterize the connectedness and zero-trust limits. The original scalar personalization model is recovered as a one-dimensional restriction. The framework therefore replaces a population-wide price-dispersion measure with a network-sensitive measure of perceived unfairness and provides a tractable foundation for studying how social structure shapes the optimal allocation of personalized prices.

detail.abstract: Problem definition. A seller may set a launch price before independent influencers publish their reviews. Influencers can reach different audiences and give different assessments of the same product test. We study when a second influencer benefits a seller that posts one price for all consumers. Methodology/results. We develop an analytical model in which consumers use their impressions of influencers to choose whose review to read and to interpret it. When all consumers read a review, competing influencers choose distinct standards, and readers adjust only partly for the standards' effects, the two reviews move optimistic and skeptical readers' purchase beliefs in opposite directions. At the same expected coverage, two influencers support a higher price below half the market and a lower price above half. Broad sales become more valuable as expected quality rises. The seller earns more with two influencers below a unique threshold in expected quality and more with one above it. Stronger source impressions can widen the gap between published reviews while reducing the additional effect of a second influencer on purchase beliefs. Managerial implications. For launch pricing, a favorable review can support a high price among a narrow group of buyers. A seller seeking broad coverage also needs to account for the more cautious assessment and how its readers interpret it. The review environment that raises seller profit can also lower expected realized purchase surplus.

detail.abstract: AIAS 1.0 established Presence, how often a fixed panel of large language models names a brand, as a measurable component of AI Availability. This synthesis adds a second component, Consistency: how evenly the panel's models name the same brand across the same questions. The Consistency arc of the measurement program first used a coefficient-of-variation statistic, which a pre-registered test showed to be coupled to Presence (pooled ρ = 0.766), and replaced it with a mean-independent dispersion statistic, φ (pooled |ρ(φ, μ)| = 0.091). A methodology lock (v1.9) then scaled φ to 0–100, rated it only for brands named at least six times across the panel, and found that no candidate composite of the two scores both carries information Presence does not and keeps Consistency separate from Presence. The synthesis therefore reports the two scores side by side. Its outline, including the wording of its headline for every possible outcome, was deposited before a third measurement wave was scored. On five product categories (112 brands, six models), Consistency stayed separable from Presence in each wave (|ρ| = 0.073 and 0.082 in the two calibration waves, 0.189 in the confirmatory wave) and kept its brand order over 152 days beyond what the question structure alone produces (ρ = 0.647, n = 52, frame-structure p = 0.008). Presence kept its order as well (ρ = 0.954, n = 112). About half the brands are named too rarely to be rated for Consistency. The results bind to one retiring six-model panel; behavioural validity is not tested.

detail.abstract: This conceptual paper investigates the critical intersection of digital transformation and social wellbeing by scrutinizing the ethical dimensions of Marketing 4.0. While these sophisticated branding strategies offer powerful tools for consumer engagement, their application in developing, collectivist economies like Sabah, Malaysia, presents a significant ethical dilemma. Millennial consumers in this region face significant financial vulnerability, making them susceptible to the potential harms of persuasive digital marketing. Situated within the fields of Transformative Consumer Research and Consumer Vulnerability, and grounded in the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB), this inquiry argues that Marketing 4.0 strategies possess a dual capacity: they can either empower consumers and build resilient communities or exacerbate financial instability by promoting unsustainable consumption. The primary contribution of this paper is the development of an ethically-grounded framework that reconceptualises brand trust. We propose that in contexts where social wellbeing is paramount, trust must evolve beyond transactional reliability to encompass a relational component: a Brand's Impact. This framework offers critical implications for businesses and policymakers on how to leverage digital transformation not just for profit, but for the cultivation of genuinely resilient societies.

detail.abstract: Sustainability-oriented outcomes in digitally connected markets arise from the interaction of organisational practice, digital engagement, consumer cognition, evaluation and behaviour, and organisational learning, yet marketing theory explains these elements in separate streams. This article names the resulting condition the Marketing Integration Gap and presents the Sustainable Digital Marketing Engagement Framework (SDMEF) as a mid-range theory of how a sustainability-oriented marketing system functions. Five Constitutional Principles govern six Constitutional Constructs, across which an adaptive mechanism, Adaptive Feedback and Organisational Learning, operates. Eight research propositions specify the relationships among the constructs, the mechanism's moderating role and the system's recursive character: the outcomes of each cycle change the conditions of the next. Sustainable Value Creation is conceptualised as a multidimensional, system-level outcome whose long-term dimension is the system's capacity to continue creating value. Placed within the Developmental School of macromarketing, the theory treats the Critical School's question as a boundary condition.

detail.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) changes how business buyers discover, synthesize, and compare information. Yet information that is easily obtained is not necessarily evidence that can support a consequential organizational purchase.

This paper conceptualizes the decision verification gap as the distance between AI-mediated informational access and the substantiation required to judge claims, manage transaction-specific risks, and secure organizational authorization. Integrating information asymmetry, signaling theory, research on calibrated trust in AI, and organizational information-processing theory, the paper develops a process account of how this gap emerges and may be reduced.

It distinguishes five non-deterministic buyer tasks—identification, understanding, comparison, verification, and decision—and four types of friction: informational, credibility-related, evidentiary, and organizational.

The proposed dual-layer evidence architecture combines machine-readable, version-controlled factual records with human-verifiable methods, limitations, independent sources, and accountable expertise. Six propositions connect evidence quality, verification costs, expert signals, and cross-functional coordination to verifiable decision readiness.

Illustrative observations from Taiwan's technology-event and named-expert ecosystems specify potential applications but are not presented as causal case findings. A staged empirical agenda identifies units of analysis, measures, comparison conditions, falsification tests, and governance requirements.

The contribution is to move inquiry beyond whether AI systems mention or cite a supplier toward whether buyers can critically evaluate and act on its claims.

The central prediction is conditional rather than universal: AI may lower information-search costs while leaving verification and coordination costs unchanged or even increasing them, particularly in complex, high-stakes purchases.

detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has ignited intense debate regarding academic integrity, data privacy, pedagogical transformation, and institutional governance. In developing ecosystems such as Brazil, public media narratives significantly shape societal perceptions, institutional agendas, and policy responses. This paper examines how the discursive polarization between Technical-Regulatory (Hard) Governance and Socio-Educational (Soft) Governance reflects institutional readiness gaps in Brazilian higher education. Grounded in French Discourse Analysis and utilizing RQDA software, the study analyzes a purposive corpus of 12 representative articles published between July 2023 and September 2026, stratified into mainstream reference journalism (Tier 1) and specialized academic and legal media (Tier 2). Cross-referencing five a priori governance dimensions with five inductively identified emergent dimensions (power relations, media arena, corporate vs. state regulation, epistemology,and environmental sustainability) and six discursive frames, the findings reveal a clear longitudinal trajectory: public discourse evolved from technological skepticism and punitive plagiarism surveillance in 2023 toward critical epistemological reflection in 2025, culminating in normative pragmatism and institutional self-regulation in 2026.Furthermore, the results nuance the expected Tier polarization, demonstrating that while specialized media extensively address legal compliance and pedagogical redesign, both tiers converge on power asymmetries and cognitive sovereignty,while systematically neglecting environmental sustainability. The study concludes by outlining strategic implications for transitioning from reactive policing toward authentic, process-oriented assessment and proactive institutional governance in the Global South.

detail.abstract: In markets for tied goods, consumers buy a durable base good and then repeatedly purchase compatible consumables. I study how compatibility between base goods and consumables affects demand, using the U.S. razor and blade market as an empirical setting. Allowing more of a firm's consumables to fit a given base good changes demand through two channels. First, it expands the market: a base good that fits more consumables is more valuable to own, attracting new buyers and making existing owners less likely to switch away. Second, it intensifies cannibalization: owners can choose among more of the firm's consumables, so a newly compatible line takes sales from the firm's existing lines. The balance between these channels matters for interoperability policy and for firms' product decisions. Reduced-form evidence shows that compatibility shapes adoption and substitution: households that own a compatible handle more readily adopt new lines, and households substitute strongly between compatible cartridges. To separate the two channels, I estimate a dynamic demand model in which forward-looking households choose each month whether to buy a razor pack, a compatible cartridge pack, or nothing. Counterfactuals at fixed prices show that market expansion dominates cannibalization when a firm makes its product lines compatible, both across families that differ in price and quality and among similarly priced lines within a family.

detail.abstract: A lender that denies credit must state the principal reasons, and lenders that use machine-learning models often derive them from feature attributions. Since many models fit the same data equally well, the reason an applicant is given may depend on which one the lender happened to train. Using 50,738,162 mortgage applications in the public HMDA data for 2018 to 2024, this paper trains 65 models in each of fourteen year-and-purpose cells, keeps those within one bootstrap standard error of the best test AUC, and computes exact Shapley values for 256,139 denied applicants. For 31.7 per cent of them, equally accurate models name different principal reasons. The prediction, recorded in advance, that this exceeds lenders' own inconsistency fails: near-identical applications at the same lender receive different first reasons far more often, mostly for reasons HMDA cannot see. But model choice shifts the share of denials given a single notice statement by up to 20.5 percentage points, annual refits move reasons more than model choice does, and attributions modelled on the two comparison populations in Regulation B's commentary disagree for a median 22.8 per cent of applicants, about 2.3 times their own Monte Carlo error. In a comparison added after the first results, monotone constraints cut disagreement by 43.8 per cent at a cost in accuracy. Disagreement concentrates on near-tied reasons, does not shrink with sixteen times more training data in the one cell tested, and, once inputs are controlled, shows no detectable difference across the racial and ethnic groups tested. An open-source package computes every measure from any set of models' attributions.

detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic principal-agent model of decentralized platform governance where tokenholders delegate control rights to representatives with unknown productivity and alignment. When Opportunistic delegates are more productive, strong performance signals greater appropriation risk, whereas avoiding extraction builds reputation. As platforms grow, individual turnout declines, but aggregate electoral discipline can persist. Delegates weigh immediate extraction and anonymous re-entry against continued control, anticipated dismissal can accelerate attacks. These incentives can sustain recurrent build-to-steal cycles and distinct governance regimes. Simulations show that productive Opportunistic delegates can improve performance while reducing welfare, and that the welfare effects of cheaper voting and restricted re-entry depend on delegate productivity and alignment.

detail.abstract: Buildings hold around half of in-use material stocks, yet high-resolution projections of future flows remain rare. We develop the first building-level estimate of material stocks for Europe (322 million buildings, 30 countries) and run a demand-driven dynamic material flow analysis (dMFA) to 2075 at national, regional (NUTS3), 10 km and 1 km resolutions. Resolution matters: from national to 1 km, cumulative 2025-2075 material inflows rise from 9.3 to 15.1 Gt, while the share that local demolition outflows could supply falls from 71% to 37%. Two effects explain this. Per-capita stock heterogeneity can raise or lower inflows, depending on where population changes. Spatial population offsetting raises inflows with higher resolution, because surplus buildings in depopulating areas cannot house growth in nearby areas, as coarser models assume. While national models tend to underestimate demand and overstate circularity, 1 km grids over-trust high-resolution population projections; we therefore find intermediate resolutions most defensible.

detail.abstract: The selection of a training method is a strategic learning decision rather than a standalone technical choice, because a method is the mechanism that creates the learning experience through which participants move from their actual competence toward the competence standard required by the organization. This article examines four families of training methods-on-the-job training (OJT), off-the-job training (off-JT), simulation-based training, and experiential learning-and shows how they can be integrated into a learning journey. Drawing on textbook, empirical, and institutional sources, it discusses the characteristics, strengths, limitations, and conditions of effective use of each method. OJT offers contextual fidelity but must be structured to avoid inconsistent learning. Off-JT provides a space for concepts, reflection, and protected practice, and its effectiveness is associated with knowledge and skill acquisition, logistical support, participant involvement in sessions, and participation in the Training Needs Assessment. Simulation brings learning closer to reality while keeping risk under control, and its value depends on matching the level of fidelity to the learning objectives and on structured debriefing. Experiential learning, built on Kolb's four-stage cycle, turns experience into knowledge and behavior. The article also proposes four dimensions for method selection-risk, cost, competence, and transfer-and illustrates them with an integrated fictional case. No method is superior in all circumstances; careful selection and complementary combinations of methods are the key to training that genuinely improves participants' knowledge, skills, and attitudes.

detail.abstract: Institutions, in Douglass North's sense the rules of the game, are chosen behind a veil of ignorance. The problems they are built to solve outrun the settings in which they are designed. Their horizons are long, their environments are combinatorial, and the states of the world that will test them cannot be enumerated-and, following Kauffman, may not be prestatable at all-let alone assigned probabilities when they are designed. Yet the standard apparatus of institutional design, from cost-benefit analysis to performance measurement, assumes a known state space and a distribution over it. This paper proposes a criterion for the regime in which that assumption fails. It is the concept of dominance. An institution is admissible if no alternative does at least as well in every describable state and strictly better in some. Among admissible institutions no dominance relation holds; there the designer is indifferent, and says so. From this dominance principle, together with a rule that scoring is used wherever outcomes resolve and dominance wherever they do not, the paper derives the main provisions of a calibrated-judgment institution for federal acquisition: resolution from events rather than approvals, proper scoring of forecasts, option questions that score strategies for what they preserved, a ledger of surprises that measures the boundary of the describable, and a constitutional rule against targets. The principle is weak by construction. Its weakness is the point: a criterion that forces a ranking where no probabilities exist is inventing them, and institutions built on invented probabilities fail in the states their designers could not describe.

detail.abstract: Smoke from Indonesian peat and forest fires affected Southeast Asia from August to early November 2026. This note models the additional attenuation of solar output in Singapore associated with fine particulate matter above a historical seasonal reference, over the 94 days of the regional haze alert, using the open hourly air-quality record. Two published concentration-response relations are applied as their authors specify them, hour by hour and weighted by the regulator's settlement generation profile. The relation of Ford and colleagues, in which attenuation scales with air mass, gives a loss of 5.58 per cent of reference production, 31.5 GWh for Singapore's fleet; that of Peters and colleagues, which has no air-mass term, gives 4.09 per cent, or 23.1 GWh. Their fitted coefficients are almost the same, and with the air-mass term removed Ford's relation gives 4.08 per cent. Among the individual perturbations tested for the national figure, the choice of specification moves the result most: timestamp alignment, a haze-correlated output stress test, the reference years and a daily implementation each move it by 8 per cent or less. Differences among reporting zones are as large, but describe variation across Singapore rather than uncertainty. The comparison shows two transferred specifications predicting differently; whether either holds for Singapore would need observed generation, with weather and system controls, to decide.

detail.abstract: Financial narratives contain rich information about firms' performance and business conditions. Conventional text analysis often summarizes this information into numerical representations, which may not fully preserve the dynamic structure described in the narrative. In this study, we develop FinVision, a domain-specific multimodal generative model that translates financial narratives into visual representations of contemporaneous market dynamics. Using 87,940 paired observations of Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) disclosures and stock price charts, FinVision learns the average relationship between a firm's narrative account of a fiscal year and its stock-price dynamics over the same period. Given an MD&A alone, the trained model generates a text-implied stock chart, extending financial text analysis beyond numerical representations toward text-to-visual generation. We validate FinVision in two ways. First, held-out tests show that the model generates stock-chart representations that closely resemble observed charts and outperform direct LLM prompting, general-purpose text-to-image models, and the same architecture without financial-domain adaptation. Second, we examine the economic validity of the generated representations by comparing text-implied and observed stock charts. The resulting discrepancy is systematically associated with weaker investor responses around subsequent 10-K filings and with worse subsequent market and operating outcomes. Overall, our findings show how domain-adapted multimodal generative AI can create a new visual representation of financial text and provide an additional modality for studying business communication.

detail.abstract: Labor force participation (LFP), the share of the working-age population that is employed or actively seeking work, is a central determinant of labor supply, potential output, and fiscal sustainability. This paper reviews the crosscountry literature on three macroeconomic determinants of LFP: GDP growth, inflation, and income inequality. Drawing on labor supply theory, research on Okun's law and the Phillips curve, development economics, and recent panel studies [1], we organize the evidence into a transmission-channel framework and identify where findings converge and where they conflict. The reviewed studies indicate that participation is procyclical but that its response to output shocks is heterogeneous across demographic groups and surprisingly persistent; that the link between development and female participation is non-monotonic; that inflation affects participation mainly indirectly, through real wages, labor-market slack and the participation margin of the Phillips curve; and that evidence linking income inequality to participation is thinner, concentrated on women and on developing regions, and sensitive to informality and institutions. We close with policy implications and a research agenda that stresses causal identification, harmonized measurement, and interaction effects.

detail.abstract: How does the regulation of big data change the welfare consequences of market structure? In selection markets, finer data let lenders price groups of borrowers separately: this can extend credit to groups that a pooled price excludes, but it removes the cross-subsidies that pooling sustains and, under market power, enables price discrimination. We study unsecured small-business credit in China, where MYbank, the lender of the Alipay ecosystem, is the dominant supplier. A temporary cut of one-fifth in its interest rates in one province provides exogenous price variation. Lower rates increased borrowing but reduced repayment. Selection is therefore advantageous despite the lender's rich data, and demand is far from perfectly elastic. Using these estimates, we compute competition and monopoly equilibria under alternative rules governing the borrower data lenders may use in pricing. Under competition, the data rule has little effect on surplus. Under monopoly, its effects are large: unrestricted data use maximizes profit but halves borrower surplus relative to the borrower-optimal rule. That rule brings the monopolist close to competition in total surplus (88.1 versus 92.4 percent of first best), but leaves borrowers only about two-thirds of the surplus they receive under competition. Empirically, the lender charges rates well below the monopoly level, attaining 84.3 percent of first-best surplus, versus 72.4 percent for a profit-maximizing monopolist with the same information.

detail.abstract: Own rates of interest are key prices in the neoclassical intertemporal model, but from these multiple commodity rates, a uniform rate of return can only be derived by means of a money rate of interest which however remains unexplained within the neoclassical model. Like Wicksell and Keynes, Hayek established a fundamental role for the monetary interest rate. Sraffa's critic of this approach failed to grasp the macroeconomic content of Hayek's contribution. Moreover, and hardly noticed in the literature, his criticism was based on a definition of own rates that does not correspond to the standard of financial market theory. Motivated by Sraffa, Keynes used the own-rate concept in the General Theory. He became entangled in formal contradictions, switched from own rates to the notion of marginal efficiencies of assets, but failed to see the inconsistency with his own definition of the marginal efficiency of capital. Therefore, instead of presenting the foundation of a liquidity premium concept of interest, Chapter 17 ends up in analytical confusion.

Artificial intelligence has shown strong evidence of being a general-purpose technology (GPT), akin to technologies such as the steam engine and the internet in its reach and ability to reshape productivity, global comparative advantages, and the structure of labor. 

In our past work, we introduced the concept of an AI labor pyramid and proposed that the adoption and diffusion of AI relies upon innovators who drive the technological frontier, users who deploy the technology broadly, and facilitators who deploy, integrate, and enable the use of artificial intelligence (or other GPTs), and bridge the gaps between innovators and users. 

This report unpacks the facilitator layer, focusing on the workers who translate cutting-edge technologies into resources for creating broad economic gains. We propose three different domains of facilitation: social, technical, and infrastructural. All three domains serve important functions in the broader ecosystem of AI adoption. We apply these domains to 94 thousand AI-related job postings made by firms in the S&P 500, and identify emerging AI job types. We find that adoption strategies vary from sector to sector, and that AI-related jobs fill clear social, technical, and infrastructural niches.

detail.abstract:
This working paper studies the fluctuations of economic growth in Zaire, and then in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from 1980 to 2010. It extends the historical analysis carried up to 1980 by following three dimensions of each crisis: the output lost, the time needed to regain the previous peak, and the path of real GDP per capita. The study combines the BCC retrospective GDP series, five editions of the accounts by sector and the World Bank’s population estimates. Two contractions of six consecutive years, from 1989 to 1994 and from 1996 to 2001, frame the brief rebound of 1995. Between the 1988 peak and the 2001 trough, real GDP fell by 49.31%. From 2002 to 2010, it grew by 5.72% a year on average. This recovery made it possible to regain two thirds of the output lost.

In 2010, total GDP remained 16.46% below its 1988 level and GDP per capita 58.11% below it. The sectoral accounts shed light on how the crisis unfolded. In 1993, services subtracted 11.60 points from growth, while agriculture added 0.83 point. From 1994, the agricultural contribution also turned negative. The Congolese experience thus shows how much the length of the catch-up depends on the depth of the initial contraction and on population growth during the recovery.

This working paper studies economic uncertainty in Zaire, and then in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from 1980 to 2010. It brings together the 124 quarterly observations of the World Uncertainty Index (WUI), which measures the frequency of the word “uncertainty” in Economist Intelligence Unit reports, with price instability, the national accounts and the reports of the Bank of Zaire and the Central Bank of the Congo. The index poorly reflects the intensity of crises: it fell from 0.1133 to 0.0919 between 1993 and 1994, while December inflation rose from 4,651.2% to 9,796.9%, and it was zero in all four quarters of 1998, the year war resumed. Its rank correlations with the instability of inflation and copper lie between −0.05 and +0.14.

A 0.10-unit rise in the WUI is associated with real GDP growth 2.89 points higher the following year in the simple regression, but only 0.98 point higher, with an interval of −2.04 to +4.00, once current growth and copper are taken into account. For fixed investment, the slope is negative (−1.89 points of GDP for a given initial rate), consistent with the postponement of irreversible spending, but sixteen observations do not pin down its size. In an expanding-window forecasting exercise, adding the WUI brings the forecast closer to observed growth in 10 years out of 18, without reducing the mean absolute error (3.38 points against 3.31). The index is best suited to documentary use: it dates the concerns of observers, which the archives then allow to be compared with the constraints actually faced.

detail.abstract:
How are international crises transmitted to the Congolese economy, and how long does it take to regain the level of activity that preceded them? This paper studies the period 1909–2010, with antecedents going back to 1847 and a first trade observation around the panic of 1907. It brings together colonial trade archives, national accounts, the reports of the Bank of Zaire and the Central Bank of the Congo, and world commodity prices. The analysis combines event studies, local projections and the measurement of recovery times. Between 1929 and 1932, the Belgian Congo recorded a 31.3% fall in export tonnage and a 77.5% fall in import tonnage.

For the period covered by the national accounts, a ten log-point rise in the real price of copper is associated, at a one-year horizon, with a cumulative gain of 5.69 log points in the purchasing power of exports in terms of manufactured goods, with a 95% confidence interval from 2.15 to 9.23 points. The estimated response of real GDP is 1.18 points, with an interval that includes zero. Resilience also depends on the indicator chosen. After the crises of the late 1990s, real GDP regained its 1996 level in 2005. In 2010, in the national series, GDP per capita and real agricultural value added remained 11.7% and 5.3% below their 1996 levels, respectively. The recovery of national output can thus coexist for a long time with a loss of output per capita and a lag in agriculture.

detail.abstract:
How did the demand for money evolve in the Congo between the hyperinflation of the 1990s and the stabilisation launched in 2001? This paper extends the study of money demand over 1909–1980. Drawing on the archives of the Bank of Zaire, the Central Bank of the Congo and IMF monetary surveys, it reconstructs real balances in domestic currency (M1) and in the broad sense (M2) from 1980 to 2010. Between December 2001 and December 2010, the purchasing power of M1 was multiplied by 3.74 and that of M2 by 5.90, while real GDP rose by 64.8%. This remonetisation is robust to the choice of the 1990 inflation measure, whereas that choice substantially alters the comparison of balances between 1980 and 2010.

Over the 31 annual observations, growth in real balances is positively associated with GDP growth (2.81 for M1 and 2.67 for M2), but the elasticities are estimated with a wide margin of uncertainty and are halved when 1990 inflation is measured at 256% rather than 874.5%. Cointegration tests do not establish a stable long-run relationship between real balances and real income alone, and the Wald test detects no change in the coefficients around 2001. Finally, in 2009, real M2 fell by 2.0% at the current exchange rate and by 21.4% when foreign currency deposits are valued at the December 2008 rate. This 19.4-point gap shows how much currency conversion can alter the monetary diagnosis during exchange rate stress, and underlines the value, for the Central Bank of the Congo, of jointly monitoring real M1, deposits in their original currency and M2 at a constant exchange rate.

detail.abstract:
This working paper traces the history of the monetary regimes of Zaire, and then of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from 1980 to 2010. It extends the study of the Congo’s monetary regimes from 1909 to 1980 and follows the end of the zaire’s peg to the special drawing right in September 1983, the loss of control over note issue under the fiscal dominance of the 1990s, the introduction of the Congolese franc in 1998, and then the 2001 stabilisation and the implementation of monetary aggregate targeting under a float. Reports of the Bank of Zaire and the Central Bank of the Congo, legal texts and IMF programme documents are set against 31 annual observations of prices, money, the exchange rate and credit, and 240 monthly observations of interest rates.

The 2001 episode is best read at monthly frequency: average inflation falls from 18% a month in January–May to 0.71% in June–December, against an objective of 1%. Over the long run, one log point of M2 growth is associated with a 0.90-point rise in prices (95% interval from 0.55 to 1.25). After 2001 this relationship becomes imprecise over nine observations, and Wald tests reject the equality of the equation before and after the transition (p = 0.005 and 0.031). Between 2003 and 2010, strict base money growth is closely associated with M1 growth (0.86), and the cumulative response of the interbank rate to a one-point change in the policy rate rises from 0.01 point in 1991–2000 to 0.67 point in 2002–2010. In 2010, inflation returns to 9.8%, close to the revised objective of 9.9%. These results call for separately dating the central bank’s domestic commitment, the behaviour of the exchange rate and the Treasury’s financing discipline.

detail.abstract: This article develops a universal philosophical framework termed Responsible Suspension as a response to the epistemic, ethical, and ontological challenges of contemporary conditions. Against both dogmatic certainty and radical relativism, the theory argues that responsible judgment emerges through the recognition of cognitive limits, the plurality of interpretive frameworks, the uncertainty of consequences, and the structural incompleteness of knowledge. Rather than understanding suspension as indecision or passivity, the article conceptualizes it as an active intellectual practice that precedes responsible action. The framework integrates insights from epistemology, decision theory, systems thinking, ethics, and social philosophy into a unified model of subjectivity. It is argued that mature judgment requires awareness of the boundaries of competence, consideration of alternative perspectives, probabilistic reasoning, critical inversion of assumptions, and attentiveness to both immediate and delayed consequences. Responsible Suspension is proposed as a universal orientation for human agency in complex environments where certainty is unattainable but action remains unavoidable.

detail.abstract: This study examines digital banking transformation in Bangladesh, with particular emphasis on financial inclusion, economic growth, Mobile Financial Services (MFS), financial technology (fintech), Artificial Intelligence (AI), smart banking, and barriers to inclusive development. Methodology: A systematic review searched Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English-language studies (2015-2025) on digital, internet, online, mobile, e-banking, and financial inclusion. However, technological, human, economic, social, institutional, security, and trust barriers including connectivity, skills, affordability, cyberthreats, privacy, regulatory uncertainty, and rural-urban disparities limit benefits. detail.abstract: Italy has one of Europe's most highly automated manufacturing bases, yet its productivity growth remains weak. The coexistence of these two facts does not show that technology is ineffective. It shows that technical capital produces results only when it is integrated into processes, supported by reliable data, matched with the required skills and converted into repeatable performance throughout a working shift. This essay examines that transition through the practical case of collaborative robotics and connects it with recent evidence from ISTAT, CNEL, the International Federation of Robotics and Banca d'Italia. It distinguishes the purchase of an asset from an industrial application, modernisation from transformation, nominal adoption of artificial intelligence from operational use, and subsidised expenditure from a project capable of creating value. The analysis leads to a proposal for firms and industrial policy: measure the performance of the complete system, reduce the risk of first applications, support integration, skills and verification, and build learning mechanisms that make successful cases transferable. Physical AI expands the scope of automation, but it does not remove the industrial conditions on which productivity depends.

detail.abstract: Under Indian Accounting Standard (Ind AS) 115 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers), real estate firms recognize revenue upon transferring control of a property-typically triggered when the Occupancy Certificate (OC) is received rather than at the point of sale. This paper analyzes the financial impact of this accounting standard alongside the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA), using Godrej Properties Limited (GPL) as a primary case study across FY2024-FY2026. Multiyear financial and operational disclosures reveal a persistent structural divergence of 6.0x to 7.4x between annual sales bookings and annualized revenue from operations. Furthermore, a severe timing mismatch occurs in Q4, where revenue from operations consistently accounts for more than 40% of annual operating revenue. Benchmarking against Macrotech Developers (Lodha) confirms that revenue deferral is an industry-wide phenomenon, although the magnitude of divergence varies by execution and scale. These findings highlight the necessity for financial analysts and investors to evaluate cash flows, customer advances, and OC receipt timelines when analyzing the real estate industry.

detail.abstract: Reentrant manufacturing systems route parts through the same resource more than once, coupling dispatch decisions across stages and enlarging the state space. Exact optimization is therefore costly, and computational searches often return policies that are difficult to interpret. We maximize steady-state throughput in a minimal reentrant system modeled as a discrete-time Markov decision process. The system has two unreliable machines and two finite buffers. Parts visit the reentered machine twice, which decides when to load a new part or deliver a finished part. The optimal policy collapses to a threshold rule: when both actions are feasible, load while the reentrant cycle holds fewer parts than the second buffer's capacity, and deliver otherwise. Complete enumeration established throughput optimality within finite policy classes, where the rule also minimized mean work-in-process among throughput optima. A subsequent study used discounted policy iteration over a larger policy class for systems with bigger buffers and broader machine parameter ranges. All converged runs across over 400,000 configurations returned this rule. At baseline reliability with two buffers of capacity 12, the rule increased throughput by 1.72% and reduced the average within-run standard deviation of part cycle times by over 30% relative to static Load and Deliver priorities. In the studied model, the rule needs no machinestate information to choose between feasible actions, making optimal dispatching interpretable and simple to implement.

detail.abstract: Machine learning models for detecting fraudulent domains are often evaluated on datasets with structural artifacts. Using 345,814 listed scam domains from a Web3 threat feed and 11,614 legitimate Tranco domains, we present an "inflation ladder" that quantifies how evaluation choices change measured performance. A naive pipeline (full hostnames, structural features, random split) reaches ROC-AUC 0.881. Under a simulated 1:100 prevalence, the lexical model achieves Precision@1% FPR of 0.065 (vs. 0.237 for the naive pipeline). We provide evaluation recommendations and discuss implications for AML compliance.

detail.abstract: We show how investment booms can accelerate natural resource depletion through endogenous producer composition. Our setting is the mid-2010s boom in California tree nuts. The boom attracts new investors with short holding periods, who grow on low-quality land and intensively tap groundwater for irrigation. Their investment accounts for one-fifth of the decline in groundwater levels in our sample of agricultural California over 2013-2023. More generally, the environmental effects of investment booms depend on investor composition, not just scale.

detail.abstract: A subsidy is an instrument of policy, not a promise of profit. A state should incur liability for recalibrating its renewable energy support framework only where it has acted wrongfully, through retroactive clawback, arbitrariness, discrimination or disproportionate response; liability should not follow from disappointed investor expectations alone. A strict-liability reading of legitimate expectations converts the fair and equitable treatment standard of the Energy Charter Treaty into an insurance policy, guaranteeing one sector its returns whatever burdens the state and every other sector must bear. The paper begins with the support scheme as a long-term risk-sharing bargain that allocates recalibration risk to the investor, drawing on Douglas’s partial dissent in Kruck v Spain: guarantees are available, but bought, not presumed. It then tests that framework against the awards that postdate it. Mainstream v Germany adopts the fault threshold as tribunal doctrine; Strabag v Germany shows the same framework producing liability where regulatory choices were lawful but their implementation wrongful; Windstream II v Canada supplies the boundary case. The record shows a consolidating threshold rather than a completed revolution. Finally, the paper sets out a two-limb test, a commitment of the requisite specificity followed by conduct that is retroactive, arbitrary, discriminatory or disproportionate, and defends it against the indeterminacy critique of proportionality, the project-finance objection and the stability reading of Article 10(1) advanced in Cameron’s dissents. The threshold is motive-neutral, treating fiscal crisis and climate duty alike, and ACF v Bulgaria is identified as its hardest case.

detail.abstract: Federal Reserve announcements carry two messages for lenders abroad: news about future policy rates and news about the economic outlook. This paper shows that European banks price the two separately, and in opposite directions, within the same loan contract. The evidence combines a high-frequency decomposition of US monetary surprises, their estimated transmission to euro area policy news and 21,513 lender-facility observations on syndicated loans to European non-financial firms between 1999 and 2023. A one-standard-deviation increase in the transmitted policy component raises spreads by 6.5 basis points, whereas favourable transmitted information of the same size lowers them by 7 basis points. Raw Federal Reserve surprises yield the same pattern. Favourable information also supports larger facilities, tightening shifts exposure towards nonbank investors, and information is priced mainly by experienced lenders. Single-index measures of monetary news therefore conceal large offsetting effects on corporate credit.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how antitrust authorities are addressing coordinated conduct facilitated by pricing algorithms. It asks two questions: which categories of pricing algorithms are most frequently targeted in recent investigations, and which parameters can distinguish legitimate, efficiency-enhancing algorithms from practices that threaten competition. Building on the "What About Bob" test and its three initial parameters (mandatory or optional recommendations; public or confidential data; adaptive learning), the paper analyzes twelve cases from the US, Brazil, Canada and Poland. It finds that dynamic pricing algorithms and hub-and-spoke coordination dominate recent enforcement, that the nature of the recommendations and of the data used are central to the assessment, and that 58% (seven of twelve) of the cases remain ongoing. The paper then proposes five additional parameters (prior explicit collusion; recommendation by a trade association or union; awareness of collective adoption by competitors; dominant position of the adopting companies; and market efficiencies). Given the novelty of the phenomenon, it argues that, except for explicit collusive agreements facilitated by algorithms, all other cases should be assessed under the rule of reason and not under the per se rule, so as not to unduly discourage the use of algorithms and their benefits for markets worldwide.

detail.abstract: Nowcasting, broadly understood as the real-time assessment of current and near-term economic conditions, is a framework of growing importance that helps inform both economic policy decision for Governments and Central banks but also shape strategies of private institutions. In this paper, a dataset of macroeconomic nowcasting application papers is compiled and analyzed to identify the main research themes and gaps in the literature. Results find that literature is rather concentrated in nowcasting aggregate economic measures, specifically GDP which appears as the target variable in 74% of the papers examined. In terms of modelling frameworks, even though there is no consensus about the best-performing type of model, Dynamic Factor Models seem to be widely preferred as they were used in 37.5% of the nowcasting applications. However, Machine Learning applications are being increasingly used after the COVID-19 pandemic, coupled by an increased reliance in the use of alternative sources of data, which feature in an average of 51.7% of annual publications between 2020-2026, compared with 18.6% during 2010–2019. Despite advances in the field, important challenges remain, as illustrated not only by the difficulties many nowcasting models faced during periods of economic turbulence but also more recently, by the Atlanta Fed’s toolkit’s “GDPNow” nowcasting undershoot associated with differences in the classification of gold imports. Further challenges arise from the insufficiently explored limitations and potential biases of alternative data sources, as well as difficulties in acquiring historical data vintages necessary for conducting true real-time nowcasting evaluations. Against this background, future research should focus on: (i) continuing on extending nowcasting applications to underexplored variables and economies, (ii) examining the predictive properties and limitations of alternative data, and  (iii) examine the potential usefulness of evaluation frameworks that combine real-time predictor vintages with final revised estimates of target variables to assess predictive performance against their underlying economic movements while avoiding look-ahead bias, so as to avoid misguiding policy makers during periods of substantial data revisions.

detail.abstract: An opening salvo of lawsuits in U.S. courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and post-deployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor's responsibility by their intent's specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology's pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.

detail.abstract: ADHD care may reduce symptoms without resolving everyday difficulties. A person may understand a strategy yet struggle to use it when needed, particularly when the support itself requires remembering, planning, or coordination. This narrative review examines how medication, psychosocial interventions, executive self-regulation, and environmental arrangements relate to daily functioning. It proposes a functional translation framework linking available capacity, situated support, enactment, and continuity, alongside the concept of implementation burden: the work required to configure, use, maintain, and resume support, including tasks transferred to others. The review distinguishes intervention findings and clinical guidance from untested practical applications. Five propositions address discontinuation, contextual matching, cue placement, restarting after interruption, and changes in support. The framework asks whether assistance can be sustained without creating excessive demands.

detail.abstract: The log-periodic power law (LPPL) is a family of models used to anticipate the collapse of asset-price bubbles. Unlike explosiveness tests or regime-switching models, it both signals the likelihood of a bubble regime, through a confidence indicator, and directly estimates the date at which that regime ends, the critical time. We apply both capabilities to the STOXX Europe 600 and examine a novel question: to what extent do high confidence values coincide with better critical time estimates? A long-horizon multi-LPPL model (N = 124,644 calibrations) generates continuous confidence indicators for 2004–2026, which we compare with a short-horizon model (N = 24,048) using empirical p-values, random critical time benchmarks, bootstrap bias tests and fixed-event regressions. The long-horizon indicator has statistically significant predictive power shortly before labelled collapses, whereas the short-horizon indicator does not. Critical time estimates are statistically meaningful for some events, notably 2007 and 2011, but weak for others, particularly exogenous events such as COVID-19. Higher confidence is associated with less late-biased and slightly more accurate critical time estimates, suggesting that confidence indicators can help filter LPPL forecasts.

detail.abstract: Concerns about conflicts of interest have led to growing calls for asset managers to let fund investors cast votes directly at shareholder meetings. We study this reform, known as pass-through voting, in a model where market participants with heterogeneous preferences lend shares, trade, and vote. We show that it can move voting outcomes further away from investors' preferences, rather than closer, for a reason that has received little attention: the fund's manager retains control over share lending and may lend more once the votes are no longer his to cast. Because the votes attached to lent shares end up in the hands of traders whose preferences differ from those of the fund's investors, pass-through voting can leave these investors worse off, even after accounting for lending revenue. The manager, meanwhile, may embrace the reform to increase lending income. Our analyses inform the debate over mandating pass-through voting, the use of lending fees as a proxy for the value of a vote, and, more broadly, policy at the intersection of shareholder voting and securities lending.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates urban climate change and resilience in the United States focusing on the effects of urbanization on climate change, urban adaptation techniques, and urban resilience to both acute and chronic climate hazards. The analysis draws attention to the growing threats that climate change poses to American communities. Heatwaves, floods, and other extreme weather events are becoming more often and intense due to climate change, which is a growing threat to American communities. Urbanization trends in the US have a significant impact on climate change, mostly by increasing CO2 emissions and exacerbating risks associated with climate change. There are still a number of gaps in this field of study, despite its continued development: there is not sufficient recent research, there is inadequate focus on the USA, and more specificity is needed when it comes to adaptation techniques and affects that are unique to different regions. This work fills in these gaps by offering a thorough examination of urban climate change and resilience in the United States, with a particular emphasis on recent research to assure the study's applicability and timeliness. California has one of the world's highest wildfire risk regions because of its unique ecosystem and climate. The Dixie wildfire was a severe wildfire in California. Fire severity and frequency have risen in recent decades, causing massive harm to the environment and society. This paper examines the use of various spectral vegetation indices (SVIs) to map burn intensity and post-fire vegetation regeneration, such as the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR). It also discusses the wildfire using Sentinel-2 images and GIS data. Specifically, Copernicus website was used to obtain the 2021 Sentinel-2 imageries from July 1st to the 10th(pre-fire) and from October 25th to the 30th(post-fire). The Fire and Resource Assessment Program (FRAP) website was also used for obtaining relevant GIS data. There were six key aspects identified: fire perimeter, fire extent, vegetation classes, timber harvest, fire risk, and prior fire. This data was imported into ArcGIS Pro to perform various GIS operations such as clip and reclassify for obtaining the maps such as the vegetation lifeform map, fire hazard zone and fire severity mapping, and earth engine was used for several tasks, such as developing a composite image, determining the burn severity index, and assessing vegetation types. This analysis provides vital insights into the Dixie wildfire's influence on the landscape and can help guide future wildfire management methods. The paper concludes by emphasizing the relevance of remote sensing in estimating wildfire risk and allowing early identification of wildfires. Analysis of fire hazard severity zones and hot spots revealed a range of threats, from low to extremely high, with very high and extremely high threat areas being the most severely affected by the wildfire. With the help of this study, future efforts at wildfire management and mitigation will be able to better understand the magnitude of the Dixie wildfire's damage as well as the distribution of hotspots and zones with the highest fire hazard potential.

detail.abstract: Deregulation of the US natural gas industry in the 1990s enabled wholesale and retail competition. However, retail market prices are inefficient because the resulting consumption levels deviate from their efficient counterpart based on marginal cost (MC) pricing. Further, MC pricing requires retail pass-throughs of wholesale price changes. Finally, the residential LRPT estimates for wholesale price increases notably exceed those for wholesale price decreases, thus lending support to the “rockets and feathers” hypothesis.

detail.abstract: Financial crises rarely remain confined to the economy in which they originate. Through interconnected banking systems, integrated trade networks, volatile capital flows, and shared expectations, shocks that begin in one market can propagate across borders and strain the stability of institutions and households far from the epicenter. This review synthesizes the theoretical and empirical literature on how global economic shocks are transmitted and how economies absorb, resist, and recover from them, with particular attention to three domains: banking stability, international trade, and developing economies. We organize the evidence around four transmission channels (banking and funding liquidity, trade and supply chains, capital flows and exchange rates, and confidence, commodity prices, and remittances) and examine how network structure, leverage, and regulatory design shape shock amplification. The review finds that cross-border banking linkages and the global financial cycle are the most consistent drivers of rapid synchronization, that trade collapses during crises are driven mainly by demand compositional effects and supplychain structure rather than by trade finance alone, and that developing economies display pronounced heterogeneity in outcomes that is explained largely by pre-crisis external balances, currency and maturity mismatches, reserve adequacy, and policy space. We conclude that resilience is best understood as a multidimensional, state-contingent property rather than a single indicator, and we identify gaps in resilience measurement, the treatment of non-bank financial intermediation, and the evidence base for low-income countries.

detail.abstract:
Random case assignment is common in courts because it helps guard against favoritism (actual or perceived) and, in bankruptcy cases, affects ex ante incentives. Despite its importance, random assignment is failing in several major bankruptcy courts today. We show this using data on the assignment of trustees to Chapter 7 cases in Chicago, Los Angeles, and New York. These trustees audit the debtor’s finances, find and liquidate assets, and police compliance with rules. We find evidence that the random-assignment process is failing in two courts (Chicago and New York). We dig deeper into the Chicago data and find that attorneys strategically time case filings to avoid or attract particular trustees (“trustee shopping”), who differ substantially in the aggressiveness with which they audit the debtor’s finances. By contrast, among cases filed by debtors who have not hired attorneys (“pro se filers”), there is no case imbalance across trustees. Because they do not engage in manipulation, pro se filers—who account for the bottom decile
of income and asset values among Chapter 7 debtors—are most burdened by trustee-shopping. We conclude by presenting evidence that trustee-shopping is less prevalent in Los Angeles due to critical differences in its random-assignment protocol.

detail.abstract: Investors need a long-run expected return for Bitcoin, but there is no established way to set one. In practice it comes from scenario models, as in the capital market assumptions J.P. Morgan has just extended to Bitcoin, or from Bitcoin's own past growth. We test both as forecasts against the returns that followed over rolling three-to five-year periods since 2012, with gold as a control and Ether as a younger comparison. Both fail: every constant rate from 7% to 21% a year, a range covering J.P. Morgan's assumption, was beaten in about nine periods in ten, by 70-120 points a year on average, while Bitcoin's long-run average growth was almost never beaten. A simple age rule comes closest: in log terms, Bitcoin's expected return is about 5.6 divided by its age in years, a forecast of about 32% a year for September 2026 to 2031, far above a CAPM required return and what crypto holders say they expect. Gold's record fits every candidate from inflation plus 1% to 7%; Ether's is too short to test.

detail.abstract: Should the authority setting monetary policy also conduct macroprudential policy? We analyze this issue within the framework of a dynamic model in which policymakers cannot make binding commitments, the public forms rational expectations, and the use of macroprudential tools is costly. An integrated authority allows for better stabilization in the face of financial shocks. However, persistent upward pressure on credit may also provide an incentive for such an authority to reduce leverage through inflation. The public anticipates this temptation and inflation remains above target. Separation removes the temptation at the cost of weaker stabilization. Relative to a commitment benchmark, separation loses only part of the response to financial shocks, a loss that does not depend on the pressure. Integration, by contrast, loses credibility at a cost that grows with the square of the pressure. We determine the exact condition for separation to be preferable: persistent pressure must exceed a threshold relative to the volatility of financial shocks. As credit correction becomes more costly, this threshold falls and, under the conditions we establish, reaches zero at a finite cost frontier. Before that frontier, the integrated authority tightens credit beyond its target to restrain its successors' inflation incentives. The persistence of observed credit gaps motivates examining weak effective prudential correction, although filtered gaps do not identify persistent pressure itself. Political interference is one possible source of that pressure, but the core result does not depend on its political origin.

detail.abstract: Activation steering is often used to show that a concept direction in a language model controls behaviour. However, a behavioural effect alone does not show that the direction acts through the concept that names it. This study proposes the Selectivity-Effect Overlap Criterion, an evidential criterion for concept-specific causal control. A pass is strong evidence for such control, whereas a failure is not evidence of its absence. The criterion first checks that the concept rating tracks the behaviour. It then requires concept selectivity under additive steering and a specific behavioural effect at the same doses. Both requirements are tested against random directions and against optimisation-matched null directions, which are trained like the real direction but with permuted targets. An objective rule variable with known ground truth serves as a positive control. For controllability and success expectation in a two-phase decision task with two language models, the forms of evidence for concept attribution dissociate. Interchange interventions identify directions that carry each concept selectively. Under additive steering, however, these directions are no more selective than the optimisation-matched nulls, and the behavioural effect of the controllability direction exceeds random directions but not these nulls. The rule control fails the behavioural step even when the intervention acts where the choice is read. There, the full hidden state carries most of the behavioural difference between the rules, while the direction that transports the rule rating carries almost none. A representation that reports a variable therefore need not be the one that mediates behaviour.

detail.abstract: Why do firms acquire startups primarily to obtain their teams when they could hire the workers directly? Acqui-hires preserve teams, but require purchasing a firm rather than recruiting its employees. I argue that acquisition can overcome a contracting problem: hiring workers separately may fragment teams and destroy the gains from their accumulated complementarities. I identify 12,271 acqui-hires in U.S. acquisition records. Relative to matched direct-hiring events, acqui-hires preserve substantially more of the original team and are associated with nearly three times as many patents per team member within two years. COVID-19 disruptions to in-person coordination weaken the acqui-hire advantage in joint invention and shift firms toward direct hiring, consistent with team complementarity driving this organizational choice. Acqui-hires also redirect invention toward the acquirer's technology, potentially limiting diffusion to other firms. In an estimated equilibrium model, banning acqui-hires induces substantial substitution toward partial-team hiring and reduces startup entry. The resulting losses in invention outweigh the gains from preserving independent innovation direction, so both aggregate innovation production and diffusion fall. Restricting acquisitions may thus preserve independent ownership without preserving the teams responsible for innovation.

The main finding is a recurrent divergence between production and capital-income rankings. Recomputing ranks within 19 manufacturing sectors yields a positive gap in 22 of 26 years and a mean percentile of 87.7, although the gap reverses in several years. Firm-mediated output feedback is below the economy-wide median in 21 years. The findings show why industrial-policy diagnostics should distinguish production linkages from the distribution and recirculation of generated income. They do not identify causal policy effects, sectoral profitability or investment capacity. Engineering studies suggest that intermittent supply damages pipes, so rationing could raise later losses, creating a "rationing trap". Using official data for 1998-2025, no specification finds a statistically significant rise in non-revenue water after rationing (preferred model +1.0 percentage point a year, p = 0.24; volume-based measures agree), consistent with cross-utility evidence; losses instead follow a steady upward trend and, at about 1.4 m³ per customer account a day, are several times international benchmarks. A leakage model calibrated to these bounds suggests that, within rationed zones, short daily cuts can return more water as later leakage than they save unless rationing is managed. Costs differ sharply: active leakage control costs about Rs 6-14 per m³ at international benchmark prices updated to 2025, the Rivière des Anguilles Dam Rs 12-20, and pipe replacement at the 2026 programme price about Rs 77, while national losses kept rising during Rs 4.6 billion of pipe replacement in 2015-2022. A storage model tested on the 2026 drawdown gives a 24-53% chance that Mare aux Vacoas falls below its 20% operating limit around late December 2026 under current operations. Water regulation by the Utility Regulatory Authority should be made operational, with loss targets met through pressure management and performance-based leakage contracts, published seasonal rationing triggers and zone-level disclosure.

detail.abstract: Białkowski et al. Their sample ends in 2007, which leaves almost two decades of data the authors never saw. I test a simple, tradable version of the effect: buy the index at the last close before Ramadan begins and sell at the last close of the month. Each Ramadan return is compared with 5,000 sets of random windows of identical length drawn from the same market, which gives a non-parametric one-sided p-value. On the main indices of Turkey, Malaysia and Indonesia, pooled with equal weight, Ramadan windows earned 5.27% against 1.69% for random windows in 1989-2007 (p = 0.025), reproducing the original finding. The US market (SPY), used as a control, shows no effect over 1994-2026 (0.81% against 0.94%, p = 0.57). The Ramadan effect is a case of an anomaly that disappears after its sample period ends. detail.abstract: Stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value relative to a reference asset, typically a national currency. However, they can lose this peg, exposing holders to losses and disrupting the services that depend on them. And, when a stablecoin returns to its peg, what has it actually recovered? Indeed, its price, backing, services, and holders' access to repayment can follow different recovery paths—or no recovery at all. We examine 57 documented incidents to understand what triggers instability, how stablecoin designs transmit disruptions, which responses are implemented, and what recovers afterward. We combine public evidence with original analyses of historical prices, collateral and debt positions, and token transactions. We classify initiating triggers and implemented responses, link them to design dependencies, and assess price, backing, redemption access, and operations separately. Backing requirements leave important vulnerabilities unresolved: security failures initiated 10 of the 28 incidents involving designs requiring full collateralization. Operational recovery does not establish price recovery: five of the 15 records with restored operations had impaired price endpoints at their respective assessment dates. Repairing a system can restore services without replacing lost assets or resolving losses. Closure can preserve an exit: all four deliberate-discontinuation incidents maintained backing and redemption access. Together, our analyses show why recovery must be assessed beyond the peg and the survival of the product. The framework makes that assessment concrete: what was restored, which holders can recover their funds, and what remains unresolved. Such findings inform stablecoin safeguards and recovery mechanisms.

detail.abstract: Momentum recurs across markets and generations, but its investment value depends on the signal, the resulting positions and the losses investors must withstand. Relative momentum ranks assets; time-series momentum changes directional exposure; adding a trend sleeve to an existing portfolio poses a separate funding decision. Drawing on studies reaching back to 1880, independently calculated U.S. stock and industry evidence, and a reanalysis of published multi-asset trend factors, this Foundation paper examines both continuation and sharp reversals. It also tests a fixed 12-month own-trend rule that switches between the U.S. research-market portfolio and Treasury bills over July 1927–September 2026. With an illustrative 10-basis-point charge on changes in allocation, the rule earned 10.22% compound annual growth, close to the market's 10.26%, while maximum drawdown was −44.50% versus −83.65% for buy and hold. A static allocation matched to the rule's 75.6% average equity exposure earned 8.85% annually with a −73.00% maximum drawdown. The rule missed swift rebounds and did not outperform the static alternative in every period. Across this nearly century-long research sample, a fixed response to sustained market weakness substantially reduced the worst loss without materially sacrificing compound growth. The result is economically meaningful in this historical portfolio comparison, but it is not guaranteed protection or an executable ETF return history.

detail.abstract: Energy firms exhibit a propensity to make payouts similar to that of industrials, but their payout structures differ markedly. They rely heavily on dividends and engage in stock repurchases only infrequently. During oil price decline, energy firms are willing to sacrifice repurchases to preserve dividends. detail.abstract: A quoted funding-rate differential is not, by itself, a measure of the cash flow available from a cross-venue position. This paper studies executable net carry as a measurement problem: expected funding must be placed on a robust multi-day basis, evaluated at a stated position size, and reduced by fees and depth-dependent entry and exit costs before routes can be compared. Using only the methodology and reported measurements in the humarb Methodology Pack, hereafter the humarb framework, the paper formalizes a route-level framework that combines contract-identity controls, seven-day medians of paired daily funding differences, separate order-book walks for entry and exit, book-specific freshness tests, and explicit treatment of unmeasured inputs. In the full-list snapshot published at 2026-11-01 19:19 UTC, 509 of 3,164 routes had a reference estimate; among those 509 routes, 462 (90.8%) had negative estimated net income after all measured costs at USD 5,000 per side over a seven-day hold. In the separate 2026-11-01 12:00–13:05 UTC window of 343 consecutive publishes, median net-positive route counts on the reference side were 71, 69, and 106 for the reported default, USD 5K, and USD 2K categories, respectively, whereas the conservative side reported zero for all tiers.
