detail.abstract: When a private-equity sponsor takes a US public company private, how much does it pay relative to the listed market, whom does it choose, and what does the deal mean for the public holder? This paper answers with a sample built entirely from SEC filings: 814 take-private deals announced from 2012 to 2026, of which 685 completed cash deals form the analysis sample, priced against a survivorship-free benchmark of US small caps on the same quarterly dates. Three hypotheses were registered before any premium or exit timing was computed, and the offer prices and buyer labels the tests rely on were validated by hand-reading seeded samples of filings. Three results stand out. First, sponsors paid more than the listed market: the median sponsor deal was priced 19.2% above the public EV/EBITDA multiple at the same date (95% interval 7.8% to 31.3%; Holm-adjusted p = 0.023). On revenue there was no premium (-1.4%): targets earned lower EBITDA margins than the benchmark company (median ratio 0.74), so the premium is a price for margin a new owner expects to add, not for growth. Second, the pre-registered claim that the premium shrank after 2021 was not supported; the difference ran the other way (+13.7% before 2022, +38.5% after). Deal multiples held at 12.5-13.0 times EBITDA while the listed benchmark fell from 13.2 to 9.0 times: the public market got cheaper, sponsors did not pay more. In an exploratory regression the premium rose with real yields. Third, exits were a measurement problem before they were a finding. Two automated readings of filings for sponsor exits were 10-17% and about 29% precise; every result built on them is withdrawn. On a hand-read list of thirteen publicrecord exits the predicted slowdown appears in direction (4.9% against 1.8% within five years) but not in significance, and the test is reported as undetermined. Exploratory results describe the rest of the deal: sponsors chose cash-generating, low-dilution companies with less net cash than their peers and no tendency to buy after falls; offers sat a median 29% above the last price yet below the target's own three-year high in two deals of three; and for public holders a buyout was a floor and a ceiling at oncefive-year windows that ended in a take-private finished at a median of 1.19 times entry against 1.03 for all others, with fewer losses and less than half the chance of touching three times. The paper contributes a validated, filings-based sample of US take-privates, a confirmed entry premium measured against a matched public benchmark rather than other deals, and a documented case of how an automated measure can fail-and how it was caught. Code, pre-registrations and lock files are public.

detail.abstract:
A historical backtest that returns a flat or negative t-statistic for a constructive strategy, meaning a strategy built from a stated economic mechanism, is consistent with two states of the world. Either the mechanism has no edge under any conditions, or the mechanism is sound and the market condition that activates it was absent from the sample. A dead mechanism calls for settling an idea and an absent condition for testing it elsewhere, and a research process that relies on backtests alone cannot tell them apart. We argue that this confusion is one source of false nulls in quantitative strategy research.
We describe a method that combines a router, a generator and a review gate. A hypothesis-type router classifies each claim as an anomaly, a structural claim, a forward claim or a theoretical claim, and bars historical backtests for types they cannot validate. A synthetic-market generator makes the activating condition an explicit input, so that a mechanism is scored on its recovery of a planted ground truth. An adversarial-review gate downgrades circular or overstated results before they enter our research record. Four case studies from our own research program show the method at work. In the first, a rebalancing-premium construction that returned a null on US large-capitalization stocks over 2007-2026 (net -68.5 bps/yr) earns +219 ± 8 bps/yr under a planted regime in which cross-sectional dispersion mean-reverts. That figure is gross and comes from a generated single-factor market, so it is a diagnostic of the mechanism and no estimate of a tradeable return. A planted trend autocorrelation of ≈0.35 gives a premium close to the historical -68.5 bps/yr, which suggested that the historical sample was a trending regime. Measuring the regime statistic on the real panel rejected that reading: the statistic lies inside the range produced by shuffled panels. That null therefore remains unexplained, and a synthetic re-classification holds only when the planted condition is also measured in the historical sample. In a second case, a pre-registered test of a dispersion detector on real data found timing skill at the 98.9th percentile of a size-matched random control, with a standalone edge too small to trade (+26.7 bps/yr, t=0.82). In a third, adversarial review found that a synthetic validation with t=8.54 was circular by construction, because generator and estimator shared a directional signal at correlation 1.0, and the result was downgraded to a compromised pass. The paper reports a research procedure and discloses no tradeable edge.

detail.abstract: Global household net worth expanded to a record level of approximately $570 trillion-nearly five times annual global GDP-reflecting a widening structural decoupling between financial balance sheets and real productive capacity. Accounting decompositions of national accounts and the global balance sheet reveal that approximately 77% to 80% of real global wealth accumulation stems from holding gains and revaluations of pre-existing assets rather than net physical capital formation. Grounded in economic literature distinguishing rent extraction from productive value creation, this paper frames persistent balance sheet inflation as a modern regime of "financial rentierism" that distorts global capital allocation by crowding out bank credit toward real estate mortgages and financial speculation, while draining corporate cash flows into share buybacks instead of fixed capital expenditure. To address this deviation of the wealth-to-income ratio from its equilibrium range derived from growth fundamentals, the study models three macroeconomic adjustment paths: deflationary asset liquidation, prolonged inflationary financial repression, and technology-driven productivity expansion. Analyzing the divergent balance sheet structures of the United States, China, and the Eurozone, the paper demonstrates that adjustment burdens are absorbed or exported asymmetrically across core global economies. Finally, the analysis traces the cross-border transmission of these shocks to a structurally bifurcated Middle East, contrasting sovereign surplus capital-exporting economies in the Gulf with deficit and reconstruction economies in the Levant and North Africa governed by exchange rate risk premia and defensive domestic real estate rentierism, concluding with a financial and monetary architecture to enable a transition from rentier accumulation to genuine industrial recovery.

detail.abstract: The Iranian economy has been subjected to severe international sanctions, yet the micro-level dynamics of firm survival-particularly bankruptcy risk-remain understudied. Using a unique survey dataset of 486 Iranian MSMEs collected during the peak of sanctions (2019-2020), this study examines how four exogenous shocks (rising raw material costs, energy prices, exchange rate fluctuations, and labor costs) trigger bankruptcy, and how sanctions condition this relationship. Employing probit and IV-probit, we find that all four shocks significantly elevate bankruptcy risk, with IV estimates revealing that short-term buffers initially mask these effects. Crucially, sanctions function as a systemic vulnerability multiplier, amplifying the impact of these shocks. Furthermore, a significant triple interaction (Shock ×Sanctions ×Newborn) points toward a cumulative vulnerability mechanism: young and small firms, lacking liquidity and credit histories, exhibit a disproportionately higher probability of exit. While financial constraints and forced layoffs increase bankruptcy risk, profitability, production expansion, and geographic location in industrialized hubs serve as critical buffers. The findings challenge generic SME support policies, calling for age-sensitive liquidity guarantees, foreign-exchange access mechanisms, and targeted insolvency protections to preserve the productive base of a sanctioned economy.

detail.abstract: Wilhelm Meisters Lehrjahre (1795-96) is presented here as a literary staging of two anthropologies of commercial modernity that correspond to the tension later named the Adam Smith Problem: the acquisitive, deferring, ledger-keeping agent of commercial society on one hand, and the self-forming, sympathetic moral agent on the other. Employing a method of milieu-reception rather than direct influence, this paper demonstrates how Goethe forces these two distinct agents to share a single narrated world as friends, correspondents, and brothers-in-law. In doing so, the novel performs three operations no treatise could accomplish: it renders the physiological cost of the acquisitive character manifest through Werner's aging; it ironizes the aesthetic claim to a higher anthropology by revealing Wilhelm's theatrical calling as a deception of the imagination; and, in the Tower Society, it discloses apparently providential guidance as fallible institutional mediation. Written during the years when Weimar was reading Smith in translation and Schiller was analyzing the division of labor, the novel anticipates the Adam Smith Problem as a structural problem of Bildung. The ledger-keeping and self-forming characters cannot be mediated through conversation alone; their coexistence requires institutional mediation that organizes a workable settlement while openly recording its human costs.

detail.abstract:
India has expanded higher education enrolment by about a third since 2014–15, capital formation has grown in rupee terms, and national skilling programmes have scaled up. Yet unemployment rises with education: in the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) for calendar year 2025, the youth (15–29) unemployment rate is 2.3% among the non-literate and 22.3% among graduates (India Labour Observatory tabulation of the PLFS). This paper asks whether education supply, investment and skill formation are aligned with the jobs the economy actually creates. It reads official and survey series for four links of the chain (AISHE, RBI and NSO capital formation, PLFS and Economic Survey skilling data, and ILO-IHD labour-market evidence) on a common footing, and does not add series that measure different things.

Three findings follow. First, the investment record is weaker than rupee headlines suggest: private corporate capital formation was 11.0% of GDP in 2023–24 against 11.5% in 2018–19, and the 2023–24 rise was led by public-sector investment. Second, formal skilling reaches only about 5% of youth and two employability indices differ by about 14 points, so skills are poorly measured rather than proven to be the binding constraint. Third, the education gradient in unemployment fits a queue for scarce regular salaried jobs (23.6% of employment) at least as well as a general skills shortage, though current data cannot separate the two. The paper proposes a ten-indicator Education-to-Employment Scorecard and a research agenda to test the competing readings.

detail.abstract: Forest regulation is imposed on forest owners, but the innovation it may induce takes place in the mills that buy their timber. We study this vertical separation in a model with regulated timber supply, imports, and mills that choose timber-saving technology subject to knowledge spillovers. Regulation induces innovation if and only if mills' timber demand is price-inelastic, so the response is weakest where output reacts strongly to costs. Mills lose unless spillovers are implausibly strong, whereas forest owners gain when the price response exceeds their rent share, a condition that imports make harder to meet. Endogenous technology dampens the price response and reduces leakage. With knowledge as a stock, a set-aside always lowers the present value of mills' profits, while a rule that raises the growing stock increases it if the stock's marginal growth rate exceeds a threshold above the interest rate. Estimates for Sweden imply induced innovation in both pulp and sawmilling, but a much weaker response in sawmilling.

detail.abstract: Our stochastic-mechanical research programme (Andreev & Howden, 2026a) claimed that signals derived from a Bohmian and quantum-field-theoretic reading of market dynamics carry predictive information about forward returns, variance, and regime transitions. Those signals included a crash probability computed from a tunnelling (instanton) action and the spontaneous-symmetry-breaking condensate |Φ|² (the squared order parameter of a model of changes in factor structure). The others were the decoherence rate (the rate at which the leading eigenvectors of the return correlation matrix rotate between successive windows), the osmotic velocity of the Nelson decomposition (the order-flow component of drift), and path signatures (iterated-integral summaries of a price path). We registered each claim before scoring it, with its thresholds and primary outcome fixed in advance (a frozen protocol), and evaluated it at the Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2016) multiple-testing bar (t > 3). Of the eight registered claims in Table 1, none is confirmed at the registered bar under its frozen protocol. Seven are settled null or disconfirmed: five of the six that concern forward returns or crash timing, the one on forward variance, and the one on a relation between signals. On forward variance the signals degraded a HAR-RV + ln(VIX) baseline, a heterogeneous autoregressive model of realised variance augmented with the log of the VIX (Diebold–Mariano t = −1.69 on 1,861 out-of-sample days, 2019–2026). detail.abstract: Investors in 401(k) plans are shifting from mutual funds to collective investment trusts (CITs), which offer lower fees and greater flexibility in fee negotiation. We document substantial heterogeneity in the benefits of CITs: large plans pay approximately 25 basis points less in fees for CITs than for mutual funds, whereas smaller plans realize negligible savings and tend to select more expensive CIT providers. To quantify the distributional effects of CITs, we develop a structural model in which plan sponsors select between mutual funds with posted fees and CITs with negotiated fees. In a counterfactual CIT ban, annual fee payments increase by $1.5 billion for more fee-sensitive sponsors, but decrease by $0.6 billion for the less fee-sensitive ones as mutual fund fees decline. Subsidizing CIT negotiation reduces fee payments by $4.2 billion per year but shifts substantial assets toward providers subject to less stringent regulatory standards.

detail.abstract: A new spectre may soon haunt the world. Suppose artificial superintelligence arrests ageing and cures all diseases. We would become amortal: still vulnerable to accidents, violence, and catastrophe, yet freed from any biological deadline. However, no technology reaches everyone at once. Unequal access to amortality could then fracture humanity in two: mortals, who continue dying, and amortals, who have escaped ageing and disease. The resulting struggle could be extraordinarily violent: mortals may have little peaceful leverage in an automated economy that may not need them, but their grievance would be a matter of life and death. The central political question of the age of superintelligence would therefore be: who owns the means of amortality? I argue that the technologies enabling amortality would embody humanity's "general intellect": generations of collective science, medical labour, biological data, and accumulated suffering. Therefore, no private owner can legitimately monopolize amortality itself. Preventing a war over amortality requires universal access before an amortal class consolidates control.

We study how monetary policy affects household debt in areas that are more and less exposed to changes in the Federal Funds Rate. detail.abstract: Fast payment systems such as Brazil's Pix and India's UPI process high volumes of instant account-to-account transfers, which makes authorized push payment (APP) fraud a critical operational risk. This paper models how offenders reallocate effort between technical vulnerabilities and human manipulation when technical controls such as Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) tighten, and how frictions on the human channel change attack success. An asymmetric-information contest between an attacker and a victim, built on a modified Tullock contest success function, endogenizes the victim's validation cost as a function of cognitive load (λ) and technological literacy (τ); the attacker's disguise capability is α. The closed-form Nash equilibrium implies that the probability of fraud success increases in λ and α and decreases in τ, and that attack sophistication is an inverted-U function of victim vulnerability. A channel-choice extension shows that hardening the technical channel displaces offender effort toward social engineering. The equilibrium maps into a logit risk score built on behavioral telemetry proxies. A synthetic sample of 150,000 fraud attempts with a known data-generating process illustrates that classical measurement error in these proxies attenuates the estimated behavioral effects by approximately 11% at a reliability level of 0.7, in line with errors-in-variables theory. The attenuation raises the relative statistical weight of perfectly measured transaction controls, lowers out-of-time AUC from 0.761 (oracle) to 0.732, and can generate false negatives in institutional risk assessments. An institutional mapping compares recent Pix and UPI rules with the European Union benchmark. Public data from the Banco Central do Brasil show that accepted Pix fraud notifications fell from 8.7 per 100,000 transactions in 2024 to 4.1 in January-September 2026, but the decline begins before the 2025 policy interventions, so aggregate series cannot isolate causal effects. Official Indian series change definition in 2024 and do not separate authorized payments, which leaves the macro risk substitution hypothesis untested on current public records. The paper proposes a heterogeneity-robust staggered event-study design for participant-level micro-data, and the model shows that policy frictions act directly on cognitive load and cash-out costs rather than on technical authentication alone.

detail.abstract: Technology transfer in Brazilian public Science, Technology, and Innovation Institutions (STIs) is marked by a structural paradox: growing scientific excellence coexists with limited capacity to convert research outputs into innovation. This article examines a deeper phenomenon, termed Perverse Invisibility of Innovation, defined as the institutional inability to recognize, activate, and transform into impact part of the value generated within research environments. To explain this phenomenon, the article proposes three interrelated constructs: Lex Imperfecta, which describes innovation-related obligations whose non-observance produces no meaningful consequences; the Institutional Valley of Death, which represents the disconnect between inventive potential and institutional activation mechanisms; and Patent Orthotanasia, which refers to the maintenance of patents without systematic valuation, prospecting, or transfer efforts. As a positive counterpoint, Alive Thesis describes the continued evolution of research benefits beyond formal academic completion. The article argues that innovation depends not only on new tools but also on effective institutional activation.

detail.abstract: Does the global diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) extend to the creation and financing of the firms that build it? Using a novel dataset of 116,795 startups founded between 2015 and 2022 across 172 countries, we link company descriptions and financing histories to the employment and education records of founders, early employees, and potential investors. We document a stark divergence between the real and financial sides of global AI entrepreneurship. On the real side, AI startups everywhere display the hallmarks of a general-purpose technology: in every world region, they target more customer sectors than comparable non-AI startups and are more likely to sell horizontal products that apply across industries. Moreover, following the release of ChatGPT, startups whose baseline tasks were more amenable to AI expanded the breadth of their work activities and commercial staffing. Yet the financing advantage that such scalable businesses command is sharply localized. AI startups raise 151 percent more annual capital than non-AI peers in North America and 181 percent more in the Middle East, compared with 42 percent more in East Asia, 16 percent more in Europe, and no detectable premium in Africa, Latin America, or South Asia. Accounting for targeted customer markets, founder credentials, early-team human capital, and local investor characteristics explains part of the gap in Latin America but leaves the broader global divide intact. In Africa, half of all AI funding goes to basic compute and data-center infrastructure; excluding these providers reveals that African AI product startups raise 57 percent less than non-AI peers. These patterns provide an early warning that AI may reach users around the world without building firms around the world.

detail.abstract:
Prediction markets have reignited longstanding debates over the scope and limitations of insider trading regulation. Recent enforcement actions assume that trading on misappropriated information in event contracts should be analyzed under the Commodity Exchange Act ("CEA") 6(c) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission ("CFTC") Rule 180.1, which was modeled on Rule 10b-5 of the Securities Exchange Act. Yet the misappropriation theory, even as applied in the securities markets, has significant gaps and blind spots. Prediction markets exacerbate those blind spots, given the inherent differences between securities, commodities, and prediction markets.

Rather than importing insider trading doctrine and jurisprudence wholesale from the securities markets into prediction market regulation, this Article proposes a realignment of regulatory priorities, grounded in private ordering, platform gatekeeping, and market integrity. Instead of misappropriation, the Article argues that prediction market regulation should focus on conduct that genuinely threatens market integrity: traders who can influence or determine the outcome of an event ("outcome controllers"), as well as any other forms of market manipulation that distort the process by which event contracts are created, traded, or resolved. 

Misappropriation causes a private harm to the source of the information, and that harm is better addressed through contract, fiduciary duty, trade secret law, or criminal prosecution rather than through federal commodities regulation. The CFTC need not, and should not, prioritize federal enforcement of private confidentiality agreements or employment contracts. This Article argues that manipulation, rather than misappropriation, should be the organizing principle of federal oversight. We distinguish private informational wrongs rooted in misappropriation from public market harms rooted in market manipulation and illustrate that prediction markets highlight the proper boundary between insider trading law, commodities regulation, and private law. This Article offers a variety of proposals geared at realigning federal oversight priorities towards curbing manipulative activity. These include platform-collected attestations whose falsity is thereby actionable under existing law, listing standards for controllable contracts, and a statutory trading ban modeled on the Eddie Murphy Rule. The Article also proposes a self-regulatory organization to standardize and enforce these rules across platforms.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines how the growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and algorithmic management (AM) into the world of work is reshaping the conditions for the effective exercise of collective labour rights. It argues that these technologies are not merely transforming work organisation and employment relationships, but also challenging the underlying assumptions on which traditional labour law and industrial relations frameworks are built. In particular, they generate new information asymmetries, facilitate corporate fragmentation and the externalisation of labour, shift managerial control across corporate structures, and raise fundamental questions about workers' contribution to the creation of economic value through data. These dynamics risk further weakening workers' bargaining power and undermining the capacity of collective labour institutions to influence decisions governing work. Against this background, the chapter examines the EU regulatory and social dialogue landscape and draws on empirical evidence to challenge the assumption that collective labour institutions constitute an obstacle to technological innovation. It makes the case for reclaiming regulatory space for collective labour rights, identifying the need to rethink existing governance paradigms and strengthen the capacity of collective actors to shape the digital transformation of work.

detail.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents equipped with graph tools can compile structured dossiers for blockchain anti-money laundering (AML) compliance, yet evaluation remains hindered by unverifiable prose, confounded self-repair ablations, and static benchmarks. Across 1,757 trajectory-shared paired investigations on Elliptic++, Elliptic2 (including an untouched holdout), and a laundering-obfuscation suite with out-of-distribution peel ratios and cryptographic identifier hashing, we benchmark quantized 7B, 9B, and 80B open-weight models on 16-gigabyte (GB) and 80/96-GB accelerators against breadth-first search, random forests, two-hop neighbor-aggregation baselines, and validation-selected classical hybrids. detail.abstract: This paper studies the intended and unintended consequences of the Preservation of Subsoil Water Acts enacted by Punjab and Haryana in 2009. The broader lesson is that agricultural environmental policy must be designed across linked margins: crop timing, groundwater use, residue management, and crop choice.

detail.abstract: Judicial modernization in developing jurisdictions frequently stalls at the "last mile," leaving sub-national trial courts reliant on vulnerable paper-based workflows despite ambitious national digital governance mandates This study examines the institutional, architectural, and policy dynamics of bottom-up court automation through an instrumental case analysis of the Web-based Case Docket Information System (WCDIS) developed for Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch X in Cagayan de Oro City, Northern Mindanao, Philippines Following the catastrophic January 2015 fire that destroyed the Cagayan de Oro Hall of Justice and halted manual court operations local court personnel and academic developers engineered a cloud-hosted PHP/MySQL docket system prior to the regional rollout of the Supreme Court's flagship eCourt program. Using a qualitative, nonsurvey methodology combining policy document analysis, system artifact inspection, and cross-case comparative benchmarking, this paper contrasts the grassroots WCDIS against evolving top-down Philippine ICT and judicial frameworks from Executive Order No. 265 (Government Information Systems Plan) and the E-Government Master Plan (EGMP) to the Supreme Court's Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations (SPJI) 2022-2027 and eCourt PH 2.0 (Supreme Court of the Philippines, 2022, 2023) as well as established international benchmarks, specifically the U.S. Federal Courts' Case Management/Electronic Case Files (CM/ECF) and the Florida Drug Court Case Management System. Findings reveal a critical trade-off between, on the one hand, agility and disaster resilience, and, on the other, data sovereignty, cryptographic integrity, and enterprise interoperability. To resolve this tension, the study proposes a Four-Pillar Resilient E-Justice Architecture designed to safely bridge grassroots regional innovations with centralized national judicial infrastructure.

detail.abstract: Trial court congestion in developing jurisdictions stems not only from high filing volumes, but also from passive information systems that function solely as digital filing cabinets rather than active decision-support tools. In the Philippines, regional trial courts manage heavy dockets dominated by narcotics prosecutions and detention-sensitive criminal cases, where manual tracking of statutory timelines risks prolonged preventive imprisonment and procedural bottlenecks. Building upon an instrumental documentary analysis of the Webbased Case Docket Information System (WCDIS) deployed in Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch X in Cagayan de Oro City, Northern Mindanao, this study employs a Design Science Research (DSR) architectural approach to conceptualize an Intelligent Docket Triage and Predictive Analytics Framework (IDTPAF). Rather than relying on user perception surveys or retrospective statistical modeling, this paper formalizes a four-layer socio-technical architecture comprising: (1) an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Legal Natural Language Processing (NLP) intake pipeline for automated metadata extraction from scanned pleadings; (2) a deterministic rule-based compliance engine for monitoring detention thresholds and speedy-trial milestones; (3) a feature-engineered predictive scheduling layer grounded in existing docket schemas; and (4) an explainable human-in-the-loop judicial dashboard aligned with the Philippine Supreme Court's Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations (SPJI) 2022-2027 and eCourt PH 2.0. The resulting blueprint provides a replicable, privacy-compliant roadmap for upgrading legacy court databases into proactive judicial management instruments in resource-constrained jurisdictions.

detail.abstract:
One agent's expenditure becomes another's income. When aggregation removes the relationships carrying that flow, microeconomic choices can become disconnected from macroeconomic outcomes. This paper distinguishes two levels of decoupling: the model first omits economic relationships relevant to its task, and its microeconomic reasoning then fails to explain the aggregate result. Drawing on entropy-governed economics, we treat transaction links, cash-flow timing, credit exposures, and local constraints as a mesoscopic layer connecting individual behavior to aggregate outcomes. The paradox of thrift shows how consistent household decisions can generate income feedback that invalidates aggregation based on fixed incomes. 

We interpret economic modeling as compression for a specified task and ask what the resulting representation must preserve. A target can be computed exactly if states assigned the same representation always yield the same target value. Under a specified finite-alphabet, independent-sampling communication model, reliable computation also requires the target's information rate to lie within the relevant cut capacity. This necessary condition does not supply an executable network protocol or ensure stable adjustment. Rate-distortion theory, maximum-entropy inference, graph representations, and communication complexity clarify these distinct requirements. Four applications examine thrift, systemic financial risk, crossborder networks and networked public goods, and aggregation topology. A model connects micro and macro to the extent that its compressed representation preserves the mesoscopic relationships relevant to its question.

detail.abstract: How do different modes of working with generative AI (GenAI) affect productivity and the experience of human workers and consumers? In this work, we examine three collaboration modes: AI-first (AI drafts, humans revise), human-first (humans draft, AI revises), and no-AI, in the context of professional writing tasks with 1,004 participants. We find that working with GenAI increased task completion time by 26% (AI-first) and 56% (human-first), due to time spent reviewing and fixing AI-generated content. Workers reported lower perceived autonomy and competence under the AI-first mode than the human-first mode. AI-assisted writing products were 60%-85% longer, more complex, and required about two higher grade levels to comprehend. Finally, a random exposure to a collaboration mode increased workers' likelihood of choosing the same mode for similar tasks in the future. Together, our findings highlight the importance of AI collaboration mode choice and the hidden costs of GenAI use on human experience.

detail.abstract: Education systems are often criticised for rewarding recall over reasoning, and Bangladesh is a frequent example. This paper asks whether the criticism holds and what it should mean for teaching now that generative artificial intelligence (AI) can answer most factual questions instantly. Drawing on learning-science research, the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 and a set of 2025-2026 studies on students' use of AI, the paper makes three arguments. First, memorization is not the enemy: retrieval practice is among the most robust findings in educational psychology, and stored knowledge is the raw material of reasoning. Second, recall alone is no longer sufficient: employers rank analytical thinking as the most important core skill, and AI makes facts cheap while making judgement about them more valuable. Third, AI can erode thinking when it replaces effort instead of supporting it, although the current evidence is early, often self-reported and based on small samples. The paper proposes a three-layer framework, Know-Question-Decide, that keeps memory in its proper place as a foundation and treats critical thinking as the goal. It closes with recommendations for students, teachers and institutions, with particular attention to assessment reform in Bangladesh.

detail.abstract: We study policy evaluation in continuous time and space with potentially non-Markovian dynamics and path-dependent rewards. detail.abstract: The healthcare supply chains have to have a compromise on the availability of products, patients safety, cost of stocks, supplier risk and response to disruption. The data on procurement, inventory, utilization, clinical and finance data in separate systems is common in hospitals and when hospital management needs to make decisions about preventing shortages or differentiate between safe cost management practices and unsafe inventory reduction. The present paper elaborates a business-analytics model of optimizing the supply chain of healthcare, controlling costs, and resilience on the side of operations. It combines descriptive, predictive, prescriptive and risk analytics in the areas of demand prediction, inventory management, strategic sourcing, supplier monitoring, product standardization, logistics and disruptive management. Four artificial quantitative characters illustrate an inventory-service boundary, probabilistic demand prediction, recovery of services following disruption and interplay involving lead time and the demand uncertainty. These numbers are fictional and a way of demonstrating techniques and do not reflect on a defined hospital, product or initial clinical test. The review concludes that analytics provides value when there is a connection between product master data, clinical use, contract terms, inventory locations, substitutes and supplier dependencies by using a governed data model. Products need to be further segmented based on clinical criticality and substitutability as opposed to having equal costs targets. Safety stock, dual sourcing, and redundancy impose apparent carrying costs to potentially minimize even bigger shortage, delaying, laboring, and patient-harm costs. Accuracy of the forecasts is not enough, hospitals will need to consider the level of service, probability of stock outage, expiry, emergency procurement, recovery time and clinical impact. The implementation roadmap that is suggested in phases includes the data and metric governance phase, the predictive and scenario models phase and must have prospective measurements of both financial and safety outcomes before scale.

detail.abstract: We study a periodic-review warehouse serving multiple heterogeneous retailers with stochastic demand and fixed costs and lead times at both echelons. We construct a deterministic echelon stock (s,S) policy whose long-run expected average cost is at most 5/2 times the optimum over all nonanticipative policies. The guarantee holds when, as in a retail chain with common service penalties, the uniform backlog penalty and heterogeneous retailer holding rates are at least the warehouse holding rate and heterogeneous retailer setup costs are at most 3/2 times the supplier’s. The latter setup-cost condition extends beyond supplier setup-cost dominance: a retailer dispatch may incur a setup cost up to 50 percent higher than a supplier order’s. Demand vectors are i.i.d. over periods with finite positive means, and demands of different retailers may be correlated. Each retailer selects the full cycle of its single-location plan or a shifted cycle of half its width, under an inflated setup cost, and the warehouse serves requests in arrival order, allowing partial shipments. The upper bound on the policy’s cost includes each retailer’s mirror cost, which prices the warehouse imbalance created by that retailer’s batching. The upper and lower bounds share a pooled supplier problem and add one problem per retailer, giving a factor independent of all lead times and the number of retailers. For arbitrary nonnegative setup costs and associated retailer demands, a consolidation policy holds allocated stock until a dispatch threshold is met and gives a factor below 4.9. On 864 instances built from Walmart store sales, the simulated cost of an integer-rounded implementation of the FIFO policy averages 1.45 times the lower bound and reaches 1.75, and our analytical upper bound on its cost is below 1.94 times the lower bound; both ratios to the lower bound have nearly the same mean at every supplier lead time.

detail.abstract: Spending used in healthcare is very concentrated, skewed, intermittent and can hardly be forecasted at the individual level. Dependable discovery of patients who are probably to encounter high future costs can be helpful in budgeting, population-health management, choosing to enter into risk contracts and specific care programs, however, predictive efficacy in itself does not designate clinical usefulness or economies. The paper is a review of the machine-learning methods to make predictions about healthcare spending and the funding of high-costs this next period. It builds up an analytical structure that isolates continuous cost forecast, classification at high cost, predicting utilization events and ranking operations. It includes the discussion of generalized linear and two-part models, penalized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks, and sequence models and ensembles and how to define outcomes, engineer features, address class imbalance, perform temporal validation, calibrate, interpret, ensure fairness, and deal with model drift. Four artificial quantitative numbers illustrate the concentration of expenditure, trade-offs between models, calibration of probabilities and expenditure capture at a given caremanagement capacity. The characters are conceptual drawings and not a perceived dataset or discoveries. There is evidence indicating that tree-based procedures often work better with structured claims data on tree-based methods compared to simple regression, whereas deep learning can be most effective when the longitudinal sequences have information that cannot be summarized by simple methods. Prior cost and utilization still are a very influential predictor but persistence is a significant base and can hide a small incremental value. Decision consistent measures should be used to evaluate models: precision at capacity, expenditure capture, calibration, net benefit and yield of intervention. It postulates a staged-governing paradigm of transitioning past-based development to a prospectively tracked implementation unconfused with the foreseeable cost and avertable one or the necessity in a patient.

detail.abstract: Higher education institutions rely on increasingly complex information systems to support academic operations, student services, institutional planning, and organizational decisionmaking. Although these systems generate substantial volumes of data, institutional knowledge frequently remains fragmented across technological platforms, administrative structures, and organizational processes. Advances in artificial intelligence, including large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge graphs, and autonomous agents, present opportunities to reconsider how institutions organize, contextualize, and operationalize enterprise knowledge. This conceptual paper proposes the Context-Aware Institutional Intelligence Framework (CAIIF), a multidimensional theoretical model designed to explain the integration of enterprise data, institutional knowledge, artificial intelligence, and organizational governance within higher education. Drawing upon organizational knowledge creation, dynamic capabilities, sociotechnical systems theory, and information systems success research, the framework defines institutional context explicitly and identifies five interconnected architectural layers and a cross-cutting governance structure. The paper advances six theoretical propositions concerning semantic interoperability, knowledge quality, contextual intelligence, AI governance, human-AI collaboration, and organizational adaptability. A complementary five-stage institutional maturity model is proposed as a heuristic to characterize conditions ranging from fragmented information environments to adaptive, AI-enabled institutional intelligence, without assuming a fixed path. The framework conceptualizes institutional intelligence as a sociotechnical organizational capability rather than a standalone technological function. It has not been empirically validated, and its propositions are offered for future testing. Implications for institutional effectiveness, accreditation, student success, strategic planning, and enterprise architecture are discussed, with directions for empirical validation.

detail.abstract: Large societies must secure compliance when most conduct goes unobserved by anyone able to sanction it. This article compares three ideal-typical solutions to this problem of scaled compliance: cosmic-ritual authority, internalized supernatural monitoring, and infrastructural-algorithmic governance. It compares them on the scope of monitoring, the timing of judgment, the mediating class, dependence on belief, exit cost, and the route by which each has been challenged. As ideal types, they move judgment closer to conduct: from episodic verdicts read in events, to a deferred verdict anticipated in conscience, to continuous scoring and preemptive constraint built into infrastructure. In essential digital systems with few substitutes, the third configuration can sustain compliance with little dependence on belief or legitimacy, because the cost of leaving holds participation in place. Understanding such systems, which helped weaken earlier forms of authority, is therefore unlikely by itself to change behavior within them. Five falsifiable propositions make the theory testable.

detail.abstract: Emerging feminist scholarship on women in national security organisations in general, and in intelligence units in particular, raises contested questions about women's operational engagement and contributions. Feminist analysis has also raised critical questions about women's agency in clandestine intelligence labour, and about how authority is capped for women operators by both the institutional and the political conditions surrounding their work. Answering these questions from the actual institutional design and operations of intelligence organisations is, however, difficult: first, because of the secrecy surrounding intelligence and the information domains of security; and second, because first-hand accounts of women's experience in intelligence are rarely available. To contribute to the study of the gendered dimensions of intelligence in contemporary war and security, this article proposes the Ministry for State Security (MfS) of the German Democratic Republic as a particularly useful site of inquiry. Its archival records constitute a uniquely detailed body of institutional data for examining how women's agency and authority were historically viewed within the institution, and how women's operational capabilities benefited the organisation on the one hand while constraining their strategic and authoritative roles on the other. This examination raises the question of whether today's gender equality regimes in security organisations continue to reproduce classical male authority alongside women's operational labour. The article examines published scholarship on the MfS in English and German, particularly the work of Angela Schmole (2023) and Jordyn Bailey (2024) on the broader themes of women and the MfS, intimacy, prostitution and Stasi operations. Existing work, however, still lacks a systematic analysis of the Stasi records aimed at understanding women's agency and authority. This article adopts secrecy as its guiding conceptual premise for examining these records, and analyses how, at the individual and the institutional level, and within family and society, secrecy drives and restricts agency and authority. It proposes the Secrecy Ceiling as a name for the point beyond which women's contribution could not become authority, and adds the life as recorded to biographical research's distinction between the life as lived and the life as told. The article is the first stage of a wider project: it develops a conceptual framework from existing scholarship, which the next stage will test and refine through primary research in the Stasi Records Archive.

detail.abstract: Dollar stablecoins settle trillions of dollars annually on Ethereum, reaching 18.4 trillion USD of gross volume in January–September 2026. Yet whether this growth has produced structural concentration around dominant intermediaries or reflects programmatic arbitrage, wallet rotation and user-base expansion remains unresolved. We formulate a four-stage framework across 81 monthly transfer networks and 27 quarterly snapshots for USDT, USDC and DAI from January 2020 to September 2026 (783.6 million filtered transfers). First, we formalize four address-level graphs—gross transfers, intra-transaction netted flows, flash-mint-excluded net flows for DAI, and direct token-contract calls (a lower-bound payment proxy)—and two entity projections. Atomic round trips rose from a few per cent of gross USDC and USDT volume before 2025 to 66% and 45% in 2026, causing raw logs to overstate contract-to-contract value shares three- to fourfold and collapsing the Nakamoto coefficient to two addresses. Second, pairing percentile inequality with fixed-rank shares shows that USDT centralized across every definition and at the entity level (top-1% share rising from 89% to 97% and top 1,000 from 69% to 83%), whereas USDC's fixed-rank shares across 10 to 25,000 recipients showed no autocorrelation-robust trend (its top-10 share following a hump-shaped path with block-bootstrap p = 0.19, and its 12,500 largest holding 98% in 2020 and 97% in 2026), identifying a sixfold peripheral expansion. DAI's post-2025 concentration reflects conversion through issuer contracts. Third, the networks exhibit disassortative hub-and-spoke topology with degree tails near exponent 2 and super-linear preferential-attachment point estimates in all 78 month-pair tests (95% lower bound > 1 in 77/78), persisting for recipients after conditioning on survival. detail.abstract: Engineers who move into leadership roles are increasingly expected to lead innovation, yet most engineering curricula say little about how innovation is organized, sustained, and protected inside a firm. This paper sets out three mnemonic frameworks developed for an interactive leadership short course for practising engineers. PIANO (Planned changes, Incremental changes, All can innovate, New practical idea, Organization) describes what innovation is. CLIFF (Committed leader, Long-term perspective, Informal relationship, Flexibility, Failure accepted) describes the organizational conditions that let innovation succeed. FORM (Freedom, Order, Research, Management) describes how a leader manages creative thinkers. The frameworks are grounded in the leadership-for-innovation literature and illustrated with cases from 3M, Google, Amazon, Intel, Kodak, Nokia, and the electric-vehicle sector. We also discuss crisis-inspired innovation in light of the COVID-19 pandemic. Anonymized insession polls from a cohort of about 30 engineers show strong agreement that innovation is mainly incremental and team-based. Respondents preferred flat structures with direct access to innovators, and none supported penalizing failure. Taken together, the frameworks give engineering leaders a compact, memorable vocabulary for building and running innovative teams.

detail.abstract: India Eight thousand Mini Coopers crossed the U.S. border with parts that were illegal to import. Nobody at the top of the chain knew until a Senate committee told them. Here is how it happened, because the mechanics matter more than the headline. A small California supplier, Bourns, Inc., bought electronic components from a Chinese manufacturer, Sichuan Jingweida Technology Group (JWD), that U.S. authorities had placed on the forced-labor entity list. That California firm sold the parts to Lear Corporation, a large Tier 1 supplier. Lear built them into modules and shipped them to BMW, Jaguar Land Rover, Volkswagen, and Volvo. When the banned link surfaced in January 2024, Volkswagen disclosed it and swapped the parts. BMW kept importing. At least 8,000 Minis with the banned components entered the country, and the imports only stopped after a congressional committee asked, repeatedly, why they hadn't (U.S. Senate Committee on Finance, 2024). Every automaker involved said much the same thing: they didn't know. The flagged supplier sat three tiers down, in a layer of the network none of them could see, BMW's own Tier 3 (U.S. Senate Committee on Finance, 2024).

detail.abstract: Does the global diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) extend to the creation and financing of the firms that innovate with it? Using a novel dataset of 116,795 startups founded between 2015 and 2022 across 172 countries, we link company and financing records to the employment and education histories of their founders, early employees, and potential venture capital investors. We document a stark divergence between the real and financial sides of global AI entrepreneurship. On the real side, AI appears to generate economies of scope consistent with a general purpose technology. Across all world regions, AI startups serve broader customer markets and following ChatGPT's release, firms performing more AI-amenable tasks expanded the breadth of their work activities and became more likely to employ commercial staff. However, the financing advantage that such scalable businesses command is localized: in North America and the Middle East, AI startups raise more than twice the annual funding of comparable non-AI startups, with smaller premia of 29 and 47 percent in Europe and East Asia respectively, and no discernible premium in Africa, Latin America, or South Asia. Accounting for customer markets, founders' backgrounds, and potential investors explain little of the regional financing differences, although early teams account for part of Latin America's gap. In Africa, half of AI funding goes to computing and network infrastructure providers; AI startups outside infrastructure raise 60 percent less annual funding than comparable non-AI startups. These patterns provide an early warning that artificial intelligence may reach users around the world without building firms around the world.

detail.abstract: Digital media have become mind extensions that can select for users' weaknesses, ranging from economic manipulation and civic harms to psychological damage. We ask whether people differ in a disposition that goes with less digital harm, and hypothesize that self-transcendence loosens the stimulus-response pairings persuasive technology exploits, which we call digital immunity. Two independently recruited samples (N = 1,164; N = 1,275, the second pre-registered), fielded fourteen months apart, combined established protective and harm measures with randomized harm inductions. The registered three-factor protective structure (self-acceptance, selfknowledge, inner stillness) replicated; the four-factor harm structure was too diverse to replicate, but a narrower one did: mental captivity (shame, envy, social comparison, brooding, fear of missing out, addiction) and naivety. One relation held throughout: self-acceptance accounted for 68% of the variance of mental captivity out of sample in both studies. Induced harms moved people high and low on digital immunity by similar amounts, so no buffering was detected, but those starting closer to the absolute harm-line were naturally more likely to cross it: the pattern is one of level, not slope. Yet after a push, 365 per 1,000 in the lowest immunity quartile stood on the harmful side, against 94 in the highest. Those who start higher therefore stay farther from harm after the same push. No protective relation of usable size appeared for economic or civic harms. The results are a first step toward a concept of digital immunity, and they map where future studies should and do not need to look.

detail.abstract: Governments increasingly look to pension savings to finance national priorities: power grids, housing, defence and new technology. In the past, patriotic investing meant lending to the state, with its taxing power as collateral. Today, pension funds are asked to invest directly in projects, taking on project risk and ownership. This inaugural lecture asks what role a preference for the home country may play in a decision that must first and foremost serve the participant's pension. The answer is built around three questions: can a fund invest, may it, and may it keep doing so? First, investability lies not in the flag but in the fit between proposition and portfolio, assessed through the Investible Window: return and risk, scale and liquidity, governance and certainty, and development risk. Patriotism does not make an unsuitable investment suitable; a better-structured proposition does. Second, a survey among participants of the APG staff pension fund shows broad support for investing at home, which weakens once it costs pension: a preference is not a mandate. Third, public support differs across countries and over time, and has to be earned again and again. The paradox of patriotic investing is that the best way to mobilise capital for your country is a proposition that needs no patriotism.

detail.abstract: Cookie banners appear on websites when visitors first arrive, informing them about a site's use of cookies and tracking technologies, and often asking them whether they consent to their data being collected and shared with third parties. We use a panel of 789 U.S. Chrome users, whose online behaviors were tracked by a browser extension they kept installed for up to three months, to investigate how users interact with cookie banners in the wild, over time, across all the websites they visit. We find that users engage with only one in three banners they encounter, and do so mostly on websites that force a response; these websites register three times more banner engagement than the ones where banners can be ignored, but lose more than twice as many visitors after their encounter with the banner. Users' explicit choices (accepting or rejecting tracking) exhibit across-user heterogeneity, and are significantly influenced by whether a one-click reject option is offered. We set a single signal from the choices users make during the first third of the days we observe them, and find that this signal is consistent with about two thirds of their later encounters. We calculate that users would spend 58 percent less time on banners if websites could not force a response.

detail.abstract: Measuring the (private) economic value of patent grants has been a longstanding challenge. In a highly cited paper, Kogan, Papanikolaou, Seru, and Stoffman (KPSS, 2017) derive an estimator using the grantee's filtered abnormal stock return associated with the grant date. We show that this estimator does not measure the value of patent grants. The grantee's market equity and idiosyncratic volatility, together with the number of patents granted to the firm on the same day, explain essentially all the variation in the KPSS-estimated value of patent grants. Abnormal returns associated with patent grants do not explain the relation between the KPSS patent grant value measure and forward citations or future firm growth. Using alternative approaches, we find that the average impact of patent grant announcements on shareholder wealth is neither statistically nor economically reliably significant.

detail.abstract: Does a rise in measured household wealth signal the creation of economic value, or does part of it reflect the repricing of existing assets and a shift in who captures the gains? This paper examines that question for the United States, with China and other economies as comparators. It combines an accounting decomposition of the Federal Reserve's Financial Accounts, a decomposition of S&P 500 prices into forward earnings and valuation multiples, and harmonised World Inequality Database (WID) series on wealth, income and their distribution. Of the USD 101.1 trillion increase in U.S. household net worth between end-2016 and mid-2026, 78.9 percent was recorded as holding gains on existing assets and 20.9 percent as net saving and investment; since 2023 the saving share fell to 15.9 percent and holding gains shifted from housing toward equity-linked assets. In an accounting (not causal) sense, about 91 percent of the log rise in the S&P 500 between end-2022 and November 2026 coincided with growth in analysts' forward earnings rather than higher multiples; realised earnings growth was concentrated, and reported net income at some large firms included large unrealised gains on equity stakes. The rise in earnings and corporate profits far outpaced productivity growth, while the nonfarm labour share fell to a record low. U.S. real national wealth per adult grew 3.5 times faster than real national income between 2016 and 2024; in China the two grew at similar rates. The evidence supports the claim that most recorded U.S. wealth gains did not arise from current saving and investment, and is consistent with a shift of income from labour to capital. It does not establish a direct transfer of wealth from poorer to richer households, nor a causal role for artificial intelligence; both remain hypotheses for further testing.

detail.abstract: We extend the constant-volatility analysis of time-based short straddles in Sharma and Mathurawale (2026) by measuring option time in variance rather than clock time. Realised variance is modelled as a deterministic intraday seasonal pattern plus discrete overnight variance, and implied variance as a total-variance clock read from at-the-money straddle prices. In this setting the at-the-money straddle, its decay and the theta-gamma identity keep their closed forms with clock time replaced by remaining variance. We add a lemma for options cash-settled on a closing price averaged over the last 30 minutes, as NIFTY options were during our sample, and an exact four-factor decomposition of a short straddle's payoutto-premium ratio into a variance premium, an intraday trend factor and a convexity factor arising from the cross-day dispersion of variance, plus a small strike term. On one-minute NIFTY data from November 2023 to May 2025, 12.6% of session variance occurs in the first five minutes and overnight gaps carry 37.8% of close-to-close variance. A variance-time clock built from these patterns tracks the market's implied clock more closely than the session clock, and explains why straddles one session before expiry decay more slowly within the day. On expiry day, implied variance exceeds realised by a factor of 1.37 (volatility ratio 1.17, 95% interval 1.08-1.26); intraday trend widens moves to settlement by 1.22 (1.02-1.41); and convexity reduces the payout by 0.91 (0.86-0.97). These three significant forces largely offset, leaving a mean short-straddle P&L of 4.0% of premium that is not distinguishable from zero. The convexity effect is stronger for afternoon entries, which accounts for the direction, though not the significance, of the afternoon advantage reported in the earlier study.

detail.abstract: We develop a spectral method for pricing nonlinear range accruals under local volatility that is piecewise constant in price and time. The method computes the Fourier transform of accrued time using eigenfunctions of the diffusion operator, supplemented by functions that account for derivative discontinuities at the corridor edges. Matrix exponentials propagate the solution within each time interval, while changes of basis connect successive intervals. Fourier inversion gives prices for contracts whose accrued payments are either forfeited or retained after a barrier hit. Probability masses at zero and full accrual are evaluated separately. At matched accuracy, the method is faster than the two finite-difference solvers considered in our tests.

detail.abstract: New ideas come from combining existing ones, so growth depends on whether knowledge reaches those who can use it. We use citation networks for two million articles in six disciplines (economics, physics, mathematics, political science, sociology and psychology) over the period 1970-2022 to study the role of academic journals in knowledge diffusion. We establish five novel stylized facts about the role of general vs field journals in these disciplines. One, we show that general journals exhibit greater cross-fertilization: their articles are cited by a more diverse set of fields than comparable articles in field journals. Two, we establish that, in four of these disciplines, general journals offer a badge of honour: articles are more cited than comparable articles in field journals. Three, in five of the disciplines, top general journals are less open to other disciplines than top field journals and they tend to be less open in disciplines with stronger consensus on which journals confer standing. Four, top general journals are more influential in other disciplines as compared to field journals. Five, multidisciplinary journals diffuse ideas more broadly across our six disciplines than general disciplinary journals, but publication in an elite multidisciplinary journal is not viewed as a signal of quality in all disciplines.
